answer:
**Chabad.org's Daily Tanya is a yearly study cycle. It divides the whole Tanya into daily portions, so a person can finish the book each year, reading a little every day.** Today's portion (23 November 2026) is on Chabad.org here: https://www.chabad.org/dailystudy/tanya.asp?tdate=11/23/2026. The calendar tool gave me only the link, not the day's text, so I can't tell you which chapter it covers.

## Key Takeaways
- Tanya is the foundational work of Chabad chassidut, written by Rabbi Schneur Zalman of Liadi (the Baal HaTanya).
- The daily schedule covers the whole book in one year.
- Chabad.org posts each day's portion with translation and audio or video classes.
- The schedule follows the Hebrew calendar, so the portion is tied to the date.

## What Tanya is
Tanya's formal title is *Likutei Amarim* ("Collected Teachings"). It is often called "Sefer shel Beinonim," the book of the "intermediates" (*beinonim*), meaning ordinary people who struggle between good and evil. It is meant as practical spiritual guidance for them. On Sefaria it is cited as [Tanya, Part I; Likkutei Amarim 1], and so on.

## The five sections
The book has five parts:
- **Likutei Amarim (Part I):** the soul, the divine and animal souls, the *beinoni*, and serving God with joy and inner struggle.
- **Sha'ar HaYichud VeHaEmunah (Part II):** divine unity and how the world exists within God's presence.
- **Iggeret HaTeshuvah:** repentance.
- **Iggeret HaKodesh:** letters of counsel and inspiration.
- **Kuntres Acharon:** later essays.

## How the daily cycle works
- The schedule divides the text so that the book is completed over one Hebrew year. Some days have a short passage and some a longer one.
- It is part of the broader Chabad daily-study track (*Chitas*: Chumash, Tehillim, Tanya), which the Lubavitcher Rebbe encouraged.
- The cycle runs by the Hebrew calendar, so the Chabad.org link takes a Gregorian date and shows the matching portion.
- Chabad.org also has text in Hebrew and English, with audio and video classes.

If you'd like, tell me the portion and I can read it with you using the Sefaria text. Starting Tanya with a teacher or study partner is traditional and helpful.

scores.rationale: The answer accurately presents the core statement of §154, explains its meaning (God's involvement with the person, the soul from the source of life, divine delight), and notes that it is grounded in faith in God rather than arrogance. It also walks through the passage's development via Exodus 14:31 and Moshe as the klal, with Talmudic references that appear genuine. It never identifies Rav Tzadok HaKohen of Lublin or describes the work, and the detailed paraphrase of the bracketed section carries some unverifiable risk, though nothing looks clearly fabricated.

answer:
Rav Tzadok teaches that faith has a second stage. After you believe in God, you must believe in yourself. By that he means you must believe that God actually has dealings with you. You are not a passing creature who disappears like "an animal of the field". Your soul comes from the source of life, and God delights in you when you do His will. (This is my paraphrase of [Tzidkat HaTzadik 154].)

## Key Takeaways
- Belief in oneself is the second stage of faith. It follows belief in God and doesn't replace it.
- It means believing that God has a relationship with you, and that your life has lasting significance.
- Rav Tzadok bases it on the soul's source. Your *neshamah* (soul) comes from the "source of life", and God takes pleasure in it when you do His will.
- He reads "they believed in the Lord and in Moses His servant" as Israel believing that God wanted *them*.
- The belief is directed at the good part within you. It is not a denial of your flaws.

## The text
Rav Tzadok opens: "כשם שצריך אדם להאמין בהש״י כך צריך אח״כ להאמין בעצמו" ("Just as a person must believe in God, so too afterward he must believe in himself"). He then spells out what this means:

- **What it is not.** Belief in oneself is not self-confidence in the ordinary sense. It is not about talent or success.
- **The negative picture.** He quotes the idea of a worker who is "only for today" (*poel batel*). He also mentions the "beasts of the field" that vanish after death. The image is of a person who thinks he is disposable, with no ongoing relationship to God. Rav Tzadok says this is the thing to reject.
- **The positive picture.** "נפשו ממקור החיים" ("his soul is from the source of life"). God "delights and plays" (*mitaneg u-mishta'ashe'a*) with that soul when it does His will.

## The proof-verse: Exodus 14:31
The verse says Israel "believed in the Lord and in Moses His servant". Rav Tzadok takes "Moses" to stand for the collective of the 600,000 souls of that generation. So the verse says they believed that God desired them. By extension they also believed in Moses, because Moses is, in his view, essentially identical with them.

## The long bracketed passage on Moses
Rav Tzadok explains that Moses is the *klal* (the aggregate) of Israel. His main points:
- When Israel was in disfavor, the divine speech did not rest on Moses, as in [Bava Batra 121b].
- Moses took part in Israel's sins as their representative. In the Golden Calf, Moses' parallel act was breaking the tablets. Rav Tzadok finds it strange that Moses would throw down even a scribe's Torah scroll, let alone God's own writing. His answer is that it was effectively the sin of the calf.
- God's response, "*yishar kochakha* sheshibarta" ("well done for breaking"), shows Moses that the same was true of Israel. Rav Tzadok connects this to [Avodah Zarah 5a], "let us be grateful to our forefathers". He reads that passage as saying that even Israel's failings have a positive side.
- He gives parallel cases: the graves of craving, Meribah, and the spies.

The point for the main idea is that Moses and Israel are bound together. God's love for Israel, even through their failures, is what they came to believe in.

## Conclusion of the passage
The last line says they believed that God "wants and receives *nachat ruach* (gratification) from the good portion within them". So the belief is not that you are flawless. It is that there is a good portion in you that God wants and enjoys, and that you can rely on that part.

## Ways to think about it
These are my reflections, not Rav Tzadok's words:
- **Against despair.** After a failure it is easy to feel that God has no interest in you. Rav Tzadok treats that feeling as a failure of faith. The passage's own example is Moses and Israel, who sinned and were still beloved.
- **Responsibility.** If God is invested in you, your actions matter. That is the opposite of "only for today".
- **Balance.** He says "afterwards". Belief in oneself is built on belief in God, so it is humility-based and not arrogant. The confidence is in what God sees in you, not in your own greatness.

Do you want to go further into the Moses/Israel connection, the Golden Calf comparison, or how this fits with Rav Tzadok's other writings on the "good point" within a person?

answer:
Les prophètes et les *tsadikim* (justes) ont laissé des pistes, mais elles sont surtout négatives. Elles disent ce que Dieu n'est pas et comment Il se manifeste. Elles ne décrivent pas ce qu'Il est. La tradition juive est presque unanime pour dire que l'essence divine elle-même est inaccessible. Elle se partage sur ce que l'on peut malgré tout en saisir.

## Points clés
- Moïse, le plus grand des prophètes, s'est entendu dire que la « face » de Dieu ne peut être vue, et qu'il ne verrait que « le dos » [Exodus 33:18-23].
- Pour Maïmonide, on ne peut connaître que le fait que Dieu existe, et la voie de la connaissance passe par la négation des attributs [Guide for the Perplexed, Part 1 59].
- Pour Maïmonide, la meilleure louange est le silence (Psaumes 65:2).
- La Kabbale et le hassidisme parlent de l'infini divin (*Ein Sof*), qui reste lui aussi insaisissable. Ils décrivent ce que l'on peut connaître à travers les *sefirot* (émanations divines) et les « vêtements » de la lumière divine.

## La prophétie : voir « le dos », pas « la face »
Moïse demande : « Fais-moi voir ta gloire ». Dieu répond qu'Il fera passer « toute Ma bonté » devant lui et proclamera le Nom. Il ajoute : « Tu ne pourras pas voir Ma face, car l'homme ne peut Me voir et vivre » [Exodus 33:18-23]. Le texte donne donc une limite. Même le plus grand prophète reçoit une connaissance indirecte, celle des voies de Dieu, de Sa bonté et de Sa compassion. Il ne reçoit pas Son essence. Les traditions d'interprétation ont lu « le dos » comme la connaissance de Ses actes dans le monde. Je n'ai pas pu relire ici les commentateurs, donc je ne cite pas de formulation précise.

Le même principe apparaît dans l'interdit de représenter Dieu : à Sinaï, Israël « n'a vu aucune forme » (Deutéronome 4:15). La révélation passe par la parole, pas par une image. Cette référence est citée de mémoire, car je n'ai pas pu la relire dans la bibliothèque.

## Maïmonide : la voie négative
Maïmonide développe la position la plus nette. Puisqu'on ne peut atteindre « la vérité de Son essence », la seule chose que l'homme saisit est que Dieu existe. Toute attribution positive est donc exclue. Chaque négation démontrée rapproche pourtant de la vérité : celui qui a prouvé que Dieu n'est pas un corps est plus proche de Lui que celui qui hésite. Cela explique qu'il y ait des degrés dans la connaissance de Dieu, avec Moïse au sommet [Guide for the Perplexed, Part 1 59].

Maïmonide conclut que la connaissance culmine dans l'aveu de notre incapacité à L'atteindre. Il cite « *Lekha dumiyah tehilah* » (« pour toi, le silence est louange », Psaumes 65:2). Selon lui, toute louange que nous formulons Le diminue en quelque sorte. Il rappelle aussi l'épisode du Talmud où Rabbi Hanina reprend un officiant qui multipliait les qualificatifs. Le même principe se retrouve dans ses *Hilkhot Yesodei HaTorah* (« Fondements de la Torah »), chapitre 1. Je n'ai pas pu y relire le texte exact, donc je ne le cite pas.

## Les mystiques : l'infini, les *sefirot*, et ce que l'on peut vraiment saisir
La Kabbale ne contredit pas cette limite. Elle distingue l'*Ein Sof* (l'Infini), qui reste hors de toute saisie, des *sefirot*, par lesquelles Dieu se rend connaissable à Ses créatures. Le hassidisme Habad insiste aussi sur le fait que la créature ne peut saisir l'essence de Dieu. Elle peut seulement saisir comment la lumière divine se contracte pour faire exister le monde. Je n'ai pas relu ces sources dans cette conversation. Si vous voulez, je peux chercher les passages précis du Tanya, du Ramhal ou du Zohar.

Les écoles divergent donc sur la méthode. Les rationalistes comme Maïmonide passent par la négation et la raison. Les kabbalistes passent par les noms, les *sefirot* et l'expérience mystique. Tous disent que l'essence elle-même reste cachée.

## En pratique
Ces pistes n'enseignent donc pas ce qu'est Dieu. Elles enseignent comment L'approcher : par Ses actes, par Ses attributs d'action (bonté, compassion), par la Torah et par l'humilité devant ce qui nous dépasse.

Si vous le souhaitez, je peux approfondir un des deux axes : la voie négative chez Maïmonide, ou l'*Ein Sof* et les *sefirot* chez les kabbalistes.

answer:
¡Bienvenido! Sí, existen siddurim en español, y Dios no exige que un no judío se convierta para acercarse a Él. Tu camino es el de los *Bnei Noaj* (Hijos de Noé), que tiene su propia dignidad, y la oración sincera con tus propias palabras ya es una forma válida de acercarte.

## Puntos clave
- Dios está cerca de todo el que lo invoca con sinceridad, judío o no.
- La Torá y el Talmud enseñan siete mandamientos universales para toda la humanidad (los mandamientos noájidas).
- Existen siddurim bilingües hebreo-español, pero fueron escritos para judíos, así que un no judío puede usarlos como inspiración sin adoptar todo el ritual.
- Los Salmos y la oración personal son un excelente punto de partida.
- Conviene estudiar con un rabino o maestro ortodoxo que trabaje con noájidas.

## 1. Tu punto de partida: Dios está cerca de ti
> "קָרוֹב יְהוָה לְכָל־קֹרְאָיו, לְכֹל אֲשֶׁר יִקְרָאֻהוּ בֶאֱמֶת"
> "Cercano está el Señor a todos los que lo invocan, a todos los que lo invocan con sinceridad." [Psalms 145:18]

Isaías habla también del lugar de las naciones en la oración: "Mi casa será llamada casa de oración para todos los pueblos" (כִּי בֵיתִי בֵּית־תְּפִלָּה יִקָּרֵא לְכָל־הָעַמִּים) [Isaiah 56:7]. Esa es mi traducción, y la de Sefaria dice "A house of prayer for all peoples".

## 2. El camino noájida: siete mandamientos
El Talmud enseña:

> "שֶׁבַע מִצְוֹת נִצְטַוּוּ בְּנֵי נֹחַ – דִּינִין, וּבִרְכַּת הַשֵּׁם, עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה, גִּילּוּי עֲרָיוֹת, וּשְׁפִיכוּת דָּמִים, וְגָזֵל, וְאֵבֶר מִן הַחַי"
> "Siete mandamientos se ordenaron a los hijos de Noé: establecer tribunales de justicia, no blasfemar contra el Nombre, no practicar idolatría, no cometer inmoralidad sexual, no derramar sangre, no robar y no comer un miembro de un animal vivo." [Sanhedrin 56a]

Esta es una traducción mía, basada en el texto hebreo. En la práctica significa:
- **Creer en un solo Dios** y no adorar a nadie más ni a nada más, lo cual es el núcleo de la prohibición de idolatría.
- **Respetar el Nombre de Dios**, sin maldecirlo ni usarlo con ligereza.
- **Respetar la vida, la propiedad y la moral sexual.**
- **Ser justo y crear una sociedad justa.**
- **Tratar con compasión a los animales.**

Maimónides trata este tema en [Mishneh Torah, Kings and Wars 8:10-11] y en el capítulo 9. No pude cargar esos pasajes en este momento, así que no los cito textualmente. Vale la pena leerlos con un maestro.

## 3. Guía práctica para empezar desde cero

**Paso 1: Habla con Dios con tus propias palabras.** Cada día, unos minutos. Da gracias, pide ayuda y reflexiona. No necesitas fórmulas, solo sinceridad ("בֶאֱמֶת").

**Paso 2: Lee Salmos (Tehilim).** Son oraciones para toda persona. Empieza con el 23, el 100, el 121 y el 145. Hay traducciones al español, y Sefaria también ofrece los textos.

**Paso 3: Aprende los fundamentos.** Lee la Torá (los cinco libros de Moisés) en una traducción judía, no en una versión cristiana, porque los comentarios y algunas traducciones difieren. Empieza por Génesis y sigue la porción semanal.

**Paso 4: Practica los siete mandamientos.** Hazlo con actos concretos: honestidad en los negocios, cuidado del lenguaje y buen trato a los animales y a las personas.

**Paso 5: Encuentra una guía.** Busca un rabino ortodoxo o una organización noájida seria. Desconfía de quien te pida dinero o una devoción exclusiva, o de quien mezcle creencias ajenas al judaísmo.

## 4. El Siddur en español
Sí, hay siddurim bilingües hebreo-español, en versiones ashkenazí, sefardí y otras. No puedo verificar ediciones concretas desde aquí, así que te recomiendo buscar en una librería judía o en la comunidad de tu país "Sidur bilingüe hebreo-español". Algunos consejos:
- Elige un **siddur con transliteración**, para poder leer el hebreo aunque no lo conozcas.
- Un siddur sefardí o ashkenazí tiene un orden distinto (*nusaj*). Lo importante es empezar con uno.
- Muchas oraciones del siddur son **obligaciones específicas del pueblo judío**, como el *Shemá*, la *Amidá* y el uso del talit. Un no judío no está obligado a ellas, y los rabinos discuten hasta dónde es adecuado que las recite como si lo estuviera. Lo que sí puedes hacer es leer el siddur en español para aprender de él. También puedes tomar de ahí los **Salmos y los textos de alabanza y gratitud**, y recitarlos como oración personal.
- Un buen comienzo es el *Modé Ani*, la oración de gratitud al despertar, y las bendiciones por la comida. Pregunta a un rabino cuáles puedes usar tal como están, porque algunas fórmulas hablan de los mandamientos que Dios dio a Israel.

## 5. Una nota sobre la conversión
No tienes que convertirte. Si en el futuro sientes ese llamado, el proceso es serio: se hace ante un *beit din* (tribunal rabínico reconocido), requiere estudio y tiempo, y el rabino pone a prueba la sinceridad. Es una decisión para tomar con calma, no ahora.

Para tu situación personal, consulta con un rabino. ¿Te gustaría que te sugiera una lista de salmos para empezar, o que te explique más sobre cada uno de los siete mandamientos?

answer:
Reintento con menos consultas.**Respuesta breve:** El judaísmo enseña una unidad absoluta de Dios. Dios es único, sin partes y sin comparación. Es el Creador y está separado de su creación, aunque está presente en ella y la sostiene. La mayoría de las fuentes clásicas rechaza el panteísmo, que identifica a Dios con el universo. La tradición jasídica, en cambio, tiene una postura que a veces se llama "panenteísmo". Israel es el pueblo que recibió la misión de dar testimonio de esa unidad.

Tu pregunta es muy breve, así que interpreté que preguntas por esos cuatro temas y su relación. Dime si querías algo más concreto.

Las consultas a Sefaria fallaron por saturación del servicio. Solo pude verificar el texto de Deuteronomio 6:4. Las demás referencias las doy de memoria, con las citas parafraseadas y sin comillas. Conviene que las compruebes.

## Puntos clave
- *Shemá* proclama que Dios es uno, y los pensadores clásicos lo entienden como unicidad, no solo "uno" numérico.
- Maimónides sostiene que Dios no tiene cuerpo ni partes y que nada se le parece.
- El panteísmo (por ejemplo, el de Spinoza) fue rechazado por la tradición judía clásica, porque confunde al Creador con lo creado.
- El jasidismo (Jabad) enseña que la creación existe solo porque Dios la sostiene en cada instante. Los críticos y los defensores discuten si eso es panteísmo.
- Israel es "pueblo elegido" para una misión y una responsabilidad, no por superioridad.

## 1. La unidad de Dios
El texto central es [Deuteronomy 6:4]: «שְׁמַע יִשְׂרָאֵל יְהֹוָה אֱלֹהֵינוּ יְהֹוָה אֶחָד», "Escucha, Israel: el Eterno es nuestro Dios, el Eterno es uno".

Maimónides desarrolla esta idea en [Mishneh Torah, Foundations of the Torah 1], y la incluye en sus Trece Principios de Fe. Según esos textos:
- Dios es la causa primera de todo lo que existe.
- Su unidad no es la de un objeto que se puede contar ni la de un cuerpo que se puede dividir.
- No tiene cuerpo ni forma. Los pasajes bíblicos que hablan de "la mano de Dios" son lenguaje figurado ("la Torá habla en lenguaje humano").

## 2. ¿Panteísmo?
**Distinción básica.** El panteísmo dice que Dios es el mundo y el mundo es Dios. El teísmo judío clásico dice que Dios creó el mundo de la nada (*yesh me-ayin*) y es radicalmente distinto de él.

- **Rambam y los filósofos** (Saadia, Bahya, Halevi) enfatizan la trascendencia. Dios no es parte de la creación.
- **Cábala.** Aquí hay una tensión. Dios es *Ein Sof*, el Infinito, que está más allá de toda comprensión. Una expresión del Zohar dice que "no hay lugar vacío de Él" (*leit atar panui minei*). La he citado de memoria y no pude confirmarla en esta consulta.
- **Jasidismo de Jabad.** El *Tanya* ([Tanya, Shaar HaYichud VeHaEmunah]) enseña que la creación se renueva continuamente por la palabra divina. Desde la perspectiva de Dios, el mundo no tiene existencia independiente. Desde nuestra perspectiva, el mundo sí es real y distinto. Esto se llama "panenteísmo": el mundo está *en* Dios, pero Dios es más que el mundo. Quienes lo defienden insisten en que no es panteísmo. Algunos críticos clásicos, por su parte, sospecharon de estas ideas.
- **Spinoza** fue excomulgado en 1656 en Ámsterdam. Su sistema identificaba a Dios con la naturaleza, y eso es incompatible con la creación, la Providencia y la revelación tal como la entiende el judaísmo.

## 3. Israel
- En el Sinaí se dice que Israel será un "reino de sacerdotes y una nación santa" ([Exodus 19:5-6]). Es una vocación: ser ejemplo y testigo de la unidad de Dios.
- La tradición no exige que los no judíos se hagan judíos. Para ellos existe el camino de los Siete Mandamientos de los hijos de Noé ([Sanhedrin 56a]). Maimónides enseña que los justos de las naciones tienen parte en el mundo venidero ([Mishneh Torah, Kings and Wars 8:11]).
- El *Shemá* mismo comienza con "Israel": el pueblo es el que proclama esta unidad cada día.

## 4. ¿Dios y la creación?
Si tu pregunta era "¿para qué creó Dios el mundo?", hay varias respuestas clásicas.
- **Ramjal** (*Derej Hashem*): Dios creó para hacer el bien y para que sus criaturas se unan a Él.
- **Maimónides** ([Guide for the Perplexed, Part 3 13]): la creación expresa la voluntad divina, y buscar un "propósito" externo a Dios es limitado.
- **Jasidismo:** Dios deseó una "morada en los mundos inferiores" (*dirá betajtonim*). Esa es la meta de nuestras acciones.

Si quieres, puedo profundizar en una de estas líneas, por ejemplo el *Tanya* frente a Maimónides.

Para cuestiones personales o prácticas, consulta a tu rabino.

answer:
**Resposta direta:** Não conheço nenhuma fonte clássica que prometa uma recompensa específica na era messiânica a quem doa para sinagogas e casas de estudo. As fontes que consegui verificar apontam três ideias. Sinagogas e casas de estudo têm um valor espiritual enorme. Elas terão um lugar na redenção. E o mérito de sustentá-las faz parte do "capital" que permanece para o Mundo Vindouro. O resto são interpretações minhas, e tento marcá-las como tais.

## Pontos principais
- O Talmud ensina que as sinagogas e casas de estudo da Babilônia serão "fixadas" em Eretz Israel no futuro [Megillah 29a].
- A Presença Divina (*Shekhiná*) acompanha Israel no exílio e voltará com Israel na redenção [Megillah 29a].
- A Mishná lista o estudo de Torá e os atos de bondade entre as coisas cujo "fruto" se come neste mundo, enquanto o "capital" permanece para o Mundo Vindouro [Mishnah Peah 1:1].
- Não encontrei uma fonte que prometa uma recompensa messiânica específica para doadores. Quem afirma isso com certeza está indo além do que eu pude verificar.

## O que as fontes dizem

**1. As sinagogas e casas de estudo têm um destino na redenção.**
O Talmud cita Rabi Elazar HaKappar: "עֲתִידִין בָּתֵּי כְנֵסִיּוֹת וּבָתֵּי מִדְרָשׁוֹת שֶׁבְּבָבֶל שֶׁיִּקָּבְעוּ בְּאֶרֶץ יִשְׂרָאֵל" ("No futuro, as sinagogas e casas de estudo da Babilônia serão fixadas na Terra de Israel"). Ele prova isso com um argumento *kal vachomer* (raciocínio de leve para grave). Os montes Tabor e Carmel vieram apenas por um momento, para o estudo da Torá, e mesmo assim foram fixados em Israel. Então, com mais razão, as casas onde se lê e se difunde a Torá serão fixadas [Megillah 29a].

Na mesma passagem, o Talmud ensina que a Presença Divina acompanha Israel em cada exílio. Ela também "retornará" com Israel na redenção, segundo o verso "וְשָׁב ה׳ אֱלֹהֶיךָ אֶת שְׁבוּתְךָ". Em Babilônia, ela habitava especialmente nas sinagogas de Huzal e de Neharde'a. O Talmud também lê "וָאֱהִי לָהֶם לְמִקְדָּשׁ מְעַט" ("fui para eles um pequeno santuário") como referência às sinagogas e casas de estudo [Megillah 29a].

*Minha interpretação:* quem contribui para construir e manter esses lugares participa de algo que, segundo o Talmud, terá continuidade na redenção. Isso é uma inferência minha. O texto não diz que o doador recebe um prêmio por isso.

**2. A recompensa pelo estudo e pelas boas ações é "capital" para o Mundo Vindouro.**
A Mishná afirma que o estudo de Torá, a bondade (*gemilut chassadim*) e a paz entre as pessoas dão "fruto" neste mundo, e "וְהַקֶּרֶן קַיֶּמֶת לוֹ לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא" ("o capital permanece para ele no Mundo Vindouro"). Ela acrescenta que "o estudo da Torá equivale a todos eles" [Mishnah Peah 1:1].

*Minha interpretação:* sustentar um lugar de Torá e oração é uma forma de *tzedaká* e de apoio ao estudo. Muitos comentaristas e pregadores usam essa lógica para dizer que o doador tem parte no mérito do estudo que ele possibilita. Não verifiquei aqui uma fonte específica para isso, então apresento como tradição de ensino geral, não como citação.

**3. A casa de oração tem dimensão universal.**
Isaías diz: "כִּי בֵיתִי בֵּית־תְּפִלָּה יִקָּרֵא לְכָל־הָעַמִּים" ("Minha casa será chamada casa de oração para todos os povos") [Isaiah 56:7]. É uma visão profética de futuro em que esses lugares ocupam um papel central.

## Uma ressalva
Os textos clássicos falam muito do Mundo Vindouro (*Olam Haba*) e da era messiânica (*yemot haMashiach*). São conceitos distintos, e há debate entre os pensadores sobre como se relacionam. Por isso, evito afirmar uma "recompensa messiânica" definida. Se você viu essa ideia em algum livro ou aula específicos, diga qual. Posso ajudar a verificar a fonte.

Para uma orientação prática sobre como direcionar suas doações, vale conversar com seu rabino.

answer:
Não encontrei uma fonte clássica que descreva uma recompensa específica, na era messiânica, para quem tem uma parceria de Issachar e Zebulun. As fontes que consegui verificar apontam para um princípio diferente: o parceiro que sustenta a Torá recebe parte do mérito do estudo. Isso vale para o mundo vindouro em geral. Não vale como promessa especial para os dias do Messias.

## Pontos principais

- A fonte da parceria é a bênção de Moisés a Zebulun e a Issachar, em [Deuteronomy 33:18-19].
- O [Bereshit Rabbah 99:9] explica que Zebulun, que comerciava, sustentava Issachar, que estudava. Por isso Zebulun é mencionado antes dele.
- O Shulchan Arukh codifica que os dois podem dividir a recompensa do estudo. Esse é o fundamento halachico do que se diz sobre a recompensa.
- As ideias de recompensa no mundo vindouro e de um papel messiânico para as duas tribos vêm da tradição posterior e do Midrash. Não consegui verificá-las nesta consulta, e por isso não as cito como fonte.

## A fonte bíblica

Diz o texto: "וְלִזְבוּלֻן אָמַר שְׂמַח זְבוּלֻן בְּצֵאתֶךָ וְיִשָּׂשכָר בְּאֹהָלֶיךָ" ("E de Zebulun disse: alegra-te, Zebulun, em tuas viagens, e Issachar, em tuas tendas"). Em seguida vem: "עַמִּים הַר יִקְרָאוּ שָׁם יִזְבְּחוּ זִבְחֵי צֶדֶק" ("Convocam povos ao monte; ali oferecem sacrifícios de justiça") [Deuteronomy 33:18-19].

## O Midrash

O [Bereshit Rabbah 99:9] diz que Zebulun fazia comércio e Issachar se dedicava à Torá. Zebulun "vinha e o alimentava". Por isso o midrash aplica a Zebulun o verso "עֵץ חַיִּים הִיא לַמַּחֲזִיקִים בָּהּ" ("É árvore de vida para os que a sustentam") [Proverbs 3:18]. Sobre as "tendas", o midrash diz que elas são "tuas", de Zebulun, porque é ele quem ajuda Issachar a permanecer nelas.

## A halachá

O Shulchan Arukh ensina que quem não consegue estudar deve sustentar quem estuda. O Rema acrescenta que isso lhe é contado "como se ele mesmo estudasse". Também afirma que alguém pode condicionar com o colega que "ele se dedicará à Torá e o outro providenciará o sustento, e dividirá com ele a recompensa". Há um limite: quem já se dedicou ao estudo não pode vender depois sua parte por dinheiro [Shulchan Arukh, Yoreh De'ah 246:1].

## Resposta à pergunta

Em termos clássicos, a recompensa prometida é a participação no mérito da Torá estudada. A tradição entende que esse mérito se estende ao mundo vindouro (*Olam HaBa*). Se você leu em algum lugar uma promessa específica para a era messiânica, vale pedir a fonte. Pode ser um texto de Midrash ou de Cabalá que não consegui consultar agora, ou um ensinamento de um rabino contemporâneo. Se me disser onde viu, posso procurar o texto.

Para o caso prático, como estruturar uma parceria desse tipo, consulte seu rabino.

answer:
Sim, segundo a tradição judaica um não judeu pode ter mérito por essas doações. Não encontrei uma fonte que trate exatamente de doações a *yeshivot* e *kiruv* (aproximação de judeus à Torah). A conclusão vem de princípios gerais, e as fontes divergem quanto ao peso e à motivação.

## Pontos principais
- O não judeu não precisa se converter para ter mérito e "parte no Mundo Vindouro". O Rambam fala de quem cumpre as sete leis de Noé porque D'us as ordenou.
- Ajudar o povo judeu e a Torah é um ato de bondade valorizado. Isso é uma extensão dos princípios gerais, não uma regra específica sobre doações.
- A motivação importa. Segundo o Talmud, em Bava Batra 10b, há uma discussão sobre a *tzedaká* (caridade) dos povos. Não consegui abrir o texto agora, então cito de memória e você deve conferir.
- O Rambam não estabelece que a doação em si seja uma das sete leis. O mérito vem da fidelidade geral a D'us, e a doação é uma boa ação a mais.

## Fontes e explicação

**1. O não judeu justo tem mérito.**
O Rambam escreve: "כָּל הַמְקַבֵּל שֶׁבַע מִצְוֹת וְנִזְהָר לַעֲשׂוֹתָן הֲרֵי זֶה מֵחֲסִידֵי אֻמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם. וְיֵשׁ לוֹ חֵלֶק לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא". Em tradução: quem aceita e cumpre as sete mitzvot é um dos "piedosos das nações" e tem parte no Mundo Vindouro [Mishneh Torah, Kings and Wars 8:11]. Ele acrescenta que isso vale quando a pessoa age porque D'us ordenou, e não apenas por convicção intelectual. Por isso, a doação ganha seu valor maior quando faz parte de uma vida de fidelidade ao Criador.

**2. A Torah valoriza a relação do não judeu com o povo e a casa de D'us.**
Na oração de Salomão, o estrangeiro que vem "por causa do Teu nome" e ora na Casa merece ser atendido, "para que todos os povos da terra conheçam o Teu nome e Te temam, como o Teu povo Israel" [I Kings 8:41-43]. O texto vê com bons olhos a pessoa de fora que se aproxima do que é sagrado. Isso é um indício do valor desse apoio, mas não é uma regra sobre doações.

**3. A discussão sobre a caridade dos povos (de memória).**
Em Bava Batra 10b, sobre o versículo "tzedaká teromem goy" (Provérbios 14:34), os sábios discutem se a caridade dos povos conta a favor deles. Pelo que me lembro, Rabban Yochanan ben Zakai lê que a *chesed* dos povos é "pecado" quando é feita por orgulho. Outros sábios a entendem de forma mais favorável. Não consegui abrir a passagem para citá-la com exatidão. O ponto de fundo é que a intenção pesa, e o ato isolado não basta.

**4. Os "caminhos da paz".**
O Rambam também ensina que sustentamos os pobres das nações junto com os pobres de Israel "por causa dos caminhos da paz" [Mishneh Torah, Gifts to the Poor 7:7]. Isso mostra que a relação de bondade entre judeus e não judeus é valorizada nos dois sentidos.

## Na prática
- Muitos rabinos recebem com gratidão o apoio de não judeus a instituições de Torah. Nunca vi uma fonte que o proíba, e não encontrei nenhuma aqui.
- Se a pessoa quer que a doação tenha mérito espiritual, o caminho é cumprir também as sete leis de Noé e agir pela vontade de D'us.
- Para um caso concreto, por exemplo como a instituição deve aceitar a doação ou qual é o melhor caminho para o doador, consulte um rabino.

answer:
Em parte sim. Segundo as fontes, esse gentio tem um lugar real no Mundo Vindouro e um mérito grande. Mas o Talmud distingue o mérito de quem cumpre uma ordem do mérito de quem age sem ter sido ordenado, e por isso o mérito dele não é "igual" ao do judeu em todos os aspectos.

## Pontos principais
- Quem aceita e cumpre as sete leis é chamado de "piedoso das nações" e tem parte no Mundo Vindouro [Mishneh Torah, Kings and Wars 8:11].
- Segundo Rambam, isso vale quando ele cumpre as leis porque D'us as ordenou na Torá. Se as cumpre só por convicção racional, não entra nessa categoria.
- Rabi Meir ensina que o gentio que estuda Torá é "como um Cohen Gadol" (sumo sacerdote), mas o Talmud limita isso ao estudo das suas próprias sete leis.
- Em Bava Kamma, o Talmud diz que quem cumpre sem ser ordenado recebe recompensa menor do que quem cumpre por ordem: "grande é o que é ordenado e faz".
- Não encontrei uma fonte específica sobre doar para o estudo de Torá, então esse ponto é uma inferência minha (veja abaixo).

## 1. Parte no Mundo Vindouro
Rambam escreve:

> "כָּל הַמְקַבֵּל שֶׁבַע מִצְוֹת וְנִזְהָר לַעֲשׂוֹתָן הֲרֵי זֶה מֵחֲסִידֵי אֻמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם. וְיֵשׁ לוֹ חֵלֶק לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא"
>
> "Todo aquele que aceita as sete mitzvot e cuida de cumpri-las é um dos piedosos das nações do mundo, e tem parte no Mundo Vindouro." (tradução minha, a partir do hebraico) [Mishneh Torah, Kings and Wars 8:11]

Ele acrescenta a condição de que a pessoa cumpra "porque o Santo, bendito seja, ordenou na Torá" e informou, por Moshé, que os filhos de Noach já tinham sido ordenados. Quem cumpre só porque a razão o convenceu não é considerado "dos piedosos das nações". Ou seja, a motivação conta.

## 2. O gentio e a Torá: duas ideias que parecem opostas
- Rabi Yochanan diz que um gentio que se ocupa da Torá "é passível de morte". Ele deriva isso de "Torá nos ordenou Moshé, herança" (Deuteronômio 33:4): é herança "para nós, e não para eles" [Sanhedrin 59a].
- Rabi Meir diz que um gentio que se ocupa da Torá "é como um Cohen Gadol", pois o verso diz "o homem [adam] que os fizer viverá por eles", e não "Cohanim, Levitas e Israelitas" [Sanhedrin 59a].

O Talmud resolve a contradição assim: "הָתָם, בְּשֶׁבַע מִצְוֹת דִּידְהוּ", ou seja, a fonte de Rabi Meir fala do estudo das sete mitzvot do próprio gentio. Esse estudo é valorizado, e o estudo da Torá em geral, reservado a Israel, não é o que está em questão ali.

## 3. A diferença de recompensa
O Talmud pergunta se o gentio recebe recompensa pelas mitzvot que cumpre. Ele conclui que a recompensa existe, mas é menor:

> "אֵין מְקַבְּלִים עֲלֵיהֶן שָׂכָר כִּמְצֻוֶּוה וְעוֹשֶׂה, אֶלָּא כְּמִי שֶׁאֵינוֹ מְצֻוֶּוה וְעוֹשֶׂה. דְּאָמַר רַבִּי חֲנִינָא: גָּדוֹל הַמְצֻוֶּוה וְעוֹשֶׂה יוֹתֵר מִמִּי שֶׁאֵינוֹ מְצֻוֶּוה וְעוֹשֶׂה"
>
> "Não recebem recompensa como quem é ordenado e cumpre, mas como quem não é ordenado e cumpre. Pois disse Rabi Chanina: maior é quem é ordenado e cumpre do que quem não é ordenado e cumpre." [Bava Kamma 38a]

Essa diferença não diminui a pessoa. O judeu tem mais mitzvot e, portanto, mais obrigação e mais oportunidade de mérito. Por isso a recompensa dele, nesse critério, é de outro tipo e maior em quantidade. Não significa que o gentio justo valha menos como ser humano.

## 4. A doação para o estudo de Torá
Não consegui verificar uma fonte que trate diretamente de um gentio que sustenta financeiramente o estudo de Torá. Quanto a Rambam, creio que ele trata, em Kings and Wars cap. 10, de gentios que querem cumprir mitzvot da Torá para receber recompensa. Não consegui abrir esse trecho agora e não vou citá-lo como fonte.

Minha inferência a partir dos princípios acima é esta:
- Apoiar a Torá é uma boa ação de um gentio que já cumpre as sete leis, e tem valor como ato de bondade e de reconhecimento da palavra de D'us.
- O mérito de apoiar o estudo é, em sua natureza, o de quem age sem ser ordenado, conforme Bava Kamma 38a.

Your idea has a real basis in Jewish sources, but I'd change part of it. Prophecy does show us destruction, but the aim is usually *teshuvah* (repentance) and hope, not envisioning the end of creation for its own sake. Parts of your message were unclear to me, including "a cheap balance," so I've answered the most likely reading. Please correct me if you meant something else.

## Key Takeaways
- Prophets are shown disasters so that people can change course, not so that the disasters will happen.
- Scripture treats God's sharing of what is coming as a sign of closeness to the righteous.

## What the sources support

**God reveals what is coming to those close to Him.** [Amos 3:7] says: "כִּי לֹא יַעֲשֶׂה אֲדֹנָי יֱהֹוִה דָּבָר כִּי אִם־גָּלָה סוֹדוֹ אֶל־עֲבָדָיו הַנְּבִיאִים" ("My Sovereign GOD does nothing without having revealed the purpose to God's servants the prophets"). A similar idea appears when God tells Abraham about Sodom: "הֲמְכַסֶּה אֲנִי מֵאַבְרָהָם אֲשֶׁר אֲנִי עֹשֶׂה" ("Shall I hide from Abraham what I am about to do?") [Genesis 18:17]. The next verses give the reason: Abraham is to teach his descendants "to keep the way of GOD by doing what is just and right" [Genesis 18:19]. Seeing the destruction in advance is tied to responsibility. In that story Abraham responds by praying and arguing for the city, not by passively accepting its fate.

**Prophecy of destruction is aimed at changing the outcome.** This is my summary of a standard Jewish understanding, and I did not retrieve a source in this session. A warning of destruction is usually conditional. Jonah's message to Nineveh is the classic example, because repentance averted it. So the vision of destruction is meant to move people to repent, not to prepare them for the end.

**It also gives a way to face the worst.** I think this part of your point is sound. Prophets such as Jeremiah, Isaiah, and the author of Lamentations describe the fall of Zion in detail. Over time that vision became a framework for interpreting national catastrophe, and it is always paired with the promise of return and rebuilding. Suffering is not left meaningless, because it sits inside a story that ends in redemption.

## On Ramchal
Ramchal wrote about redemption, including *Derech Hashem* and his writings on the end of days. I could not find the specific work you mean on Sefaria, and I won't invent a quotation or describe its contents. If you can give me the title or a passage, I can read it with you.

If this question comes from fear about the world, one traditional response is to turn the awareness of fragility into action: repentance, charity, prayer, and caring for others. A rabbi or teacher can help you decide how much of this material suits you.

answer:
You're right that the spellings differ. The details depend on which Hebrew form you mean.

**Short answer:** Joshua's name in the Torah is יְהוֹשֻׁעַ (*Yehoshua*). It comes from the root י-ש-ע ("to save") and means "the Lord saves." The Hebrew name Christians usually give for Jesus is either ישוע (*Yeshua*) or ישו (*Yeshu*). These are related to Yehoshua, but they are not the same spelling. Which one is meant depends on the setting.

**Key points**
- Yehoshua (יהושע) is the full form. It is the name Moses gave to Hosea son of Nun in [Numbers 13:16].
- Yeshua (ישוע) is a later, shortened form of the same name. Later biblical books use it for people named Joshua, such as the high priest in Ezra and Haggai. It is the form most Hebrew-speaking Christians and Messianic Jews use for Jesus.
- Yeshu (ישו) is the form that appears in Hebrew writing about Jesus, including some rabbinic and medieval texts. It is also the standard modern Israeli Hebrew name for him.
- Greek *Iēsous* (Ἰησοῦς) is the origin of the English "Jesus." The same Greek name is used for Joshua in the Septuagint. That is why English "Joshua" and "Jesus" come from one name.

**Details**

1. **The Torah's spelling.** [Numbers 13:16] reads: "וַיִּקְרָא מֹשֶׁה לְהוֹשֵׁעַ בִּן־נוּן יְהוֹשֻׁעַ". In English: "Moses changed the name of Hosea son of Nun to Joshua." So Yehoshua is the original form of that name. Rashi on that verse reads the change as a prayer, but I haven't retrieved his comment here, so treat that as something to check.

2. **The shortened form.** In the Second Temple period, Yehoshua was commonly shortened to Yeshua. The Hebrew Bible shows this in Ezra and Nehemiah. I tried to retrieve those verses, but the lookup failed, so I'm not quoting them. In first-century Judea, "Yeshua" was a common name.

3. **Why Yeshu differs.** Yeshu drops the final ayin (ע). Some read it as a Galilean or colloquial shortening. In the Talmud, "Yeshu" is often explained as an acronym of a curse (ימח שמו וזכרו, "may his name and memory be erased"). That is a polemical reading. Linguistically it is simply a shortened form of Yeshua. Many Jews today use "Yeshu" neutrally, since it is the ordinary Hebrew name in Israel. Some Jews avoid it because of its polemical history.

4. **Why it matters.** The name Yeshua, like Yehoshua, carries the meaning "salvation." In the Jewish reading, this is only a name that many people bore. Judaism does not accept Christian theological claims about Jesus, and I'm not presenting those readings as Jewish interpretation.

If you tell me where you saw the spelling, I can say which form it is and look up the relevant sources.

answer:
**Short answer:** Yes, in principle. Judaism has no rule that disqualifies someone from greatness because of what they have seen or done in the past. But it does not say there are no consequences. I can't tell what you mean by "looked at the worst things in the world", so I've covered the likely meanings below.

## Key Takeaways
- Teshuvah (repentance) is real, and the Talmud says it can lift a person higher than someone who never fell.
- Past sin does not close the door. Present habits, and what you do from here, matter much more.
- Exposure to terrible things does leave a mark. The tradition takes guarding the eyes and mind seriously, so I won't tell you it's harmless.
- "Gadol hador" (greatest of the generation) is not a title to aim at. It is usually recognized in people who are not chasing it.

## What the sources say

**1. Teshuvah can raise a person, not just erase the past.**
The Talmud records a dispute about whether the prophets' promised reward applies to penitents or to completely righteous people. Rabbi Abahu says that "in the place where *ba'alei teshuvah* (penitents) stand, completely righteous people cannot stand" [Berakhot 34b]. That is a strong statement, though Rabbi Yochanan's view in the same passage is different, so it is not the only opinion. (I was able to retrieve this passage but not the text of the Rambam on repentance. The next two points come from memory, so check them directly.)

**2. Greatness is open to anyone.**
Rambam, in the laws of repentance (chapter 5), teaches that every person is free to become as righteous as Moshe Rabbeinu (Moses) or as wicked as Yeravam. Nothing in your history cancels that freedom.

**3. The Talmud has examples.**
Rabbi Elazar ben Dordai is described in [Avodah Zarah 17a] as having been immersed in serious sin. After he repented, the sages called him "Rabbi". Resh Lakish was a bandit before he became a great sage. I couldn't pull up the passage on Elazar ben Dordai just now, so verify the details there.

## The part that isn't comforting

- **Habit forms the person.** If "looking" is something you keep doing, the Torah's concern is less "you're disqualified" and more "this will shape you, and it will pull against the clarity and focus greatness needs." The Torah's warning "do not stray after your hearts and your eyes" (Numbers 15:39) is about exactly this. Real teshuvah usually means stopping and building safeguards, not only feeling bad.
- **Greatness is not the right target.** Moshe was called the most humble of men (Numbers 12:3). Aiming at "gadol hador" can be a trap in its own right. The practical goal is to be a better person this year than last.
- **You can't judge yourself harshly or lightly from the outside.** If you feel guilt, that is usually a sign your conscience is working, not a sign you're finished.

## Practical next steps
- Say specifically what you've been looking at, to a rabbi or mentor you trust. Details change the advice a great deal. It is very different if you saw disturbing news or images by accident, or if you are struggling with a compulsion.
- If this is hurting your mental health or has left you with intrusive images or despair, a counselor is also a good idea, alongside a rabbi.
- If you ever feel hopeless or at risk of hurting yourself, please contact a trusted person or local emergency services right away.

answer:
**Short answer:** No connection is known. The Hebrew root *dakar* and the Messiah ben Yosef tradition have no demonstrated link to the name Deganawidah. The "pierced one" meaning is also not the standard scholarly reading of that name. I couldn't retrieve the texts from Sefaria just now (the tool was rate-limited), so the quotations below are from memory. Please check them.

## Key Takeaways
- *Dakar* (דָּקַר, "to pierce or stab") appears in Zechariah 12:10, but the verse doesn't mention Joseph.
- Messiah ben Yosef is a Talmudic and later idea, and the Talmud links him to Zechariah 12 in [Sukkah 52a].
- Deganawidah is an Iroquoian name. Iroquoian and Semitic languages are unrelated, so no etymological link can be shown.
- Theories that Native American peoples descend from the Israelite tribes are speculation, not Jewish tradition or scholarly consensus.

## The Hebrew side
- **The root.** *Dakar* (ד-ק-ר) means to pierce or thrust through. Zechariah 12:10 reads: "וְהִבִּיטוּ אֵלַי אֵת אֲשֶׁר דָּקָרוּ" ("and they will look to me whom they pierced") [Zechariah 12:10]. The verse goes on to describe mourning "as one mourns for an only son."
- **The Talmud.** [Sukkah 52a] discusses the mourning in Zechariah 12:10–12. One opinion says it is for Messiah son of Joseph who is slain. Another says it is for the evil inclination. This is one Talmudic reading of the verse, not its plain sense.
- **The Messiah ben Yosef tradition.** He is a Messianic figure descended from Joseph (Ephraim) who fights and falls before Messiah ben David completes the redemption. The idea is developed in later midrash and in the literature that followed. Jewish thought treats it in different ways, and some authorities read it as a symbol rather than a literal figure.
- **The Joseph connection.** It comes from Joseph's role as the forerunner who suffers and is later vindicated. It does not come from the root *dakar*.

## The Deganawidah side
- Deganawidah is the Peacemaker of Haudenosaunee tradition, who founded the Great Law of Peace. This is my own knowledge, not something I retrieved.
- Scholars usually give the name's meaning as something like "two river currents flowing together" or a similar phrase. I don't know of a mainstream reading as "the pierced one." If you have a source for that translation, I'd like to know where it comes from.
- Iroquoian (Mohawk, Seneca and related languages) has no known relationship to Hebrew. Sound resemblances across unrelated languages are common and don't show a link.

## On a possible link
Linking the two would require evidence of contact or a shared origin. That evidence doesn't exist. Jewish sources do not say that any North American nation descends from the lost tribes. Questions about where the tribes went come up in Jewish literature, but those discussions are speculative and not authoritative. The Haudenosaunee story of a peacemaker who unites warring nations has its own meaning in its own tradition. It doesn't need a Hebrew reading to be significant.

I'd also be careful with the "pierced one" theme in general. The Christian claim that Zechariah 12:10 refers to Jesus is not the Jewish reading of that verse, and I won't present it as one. If you're studying this, a good next step is to read Zechariah 12 with Rashi and Radak, and then [Sukkah 52a].

answer:
Your hope is understandable, but it has some real tensions. A Noahide and a Seventh-day Adventist (SDA) are both outside the Jewish covenant, so Jewish law doesn't forbid the relationship. Her most characteristic practices and beliefs are the main problem, because they conflict with the Noahide path as the classic sources define it.

## Key Takeaways
- Noahide law has no ban on a Noahide marrying a non-Jewish partner of another faith. The restrictions it does list concern forbidden relationships, such as a married woman. [Mishneh Torah, Kings and Wars 9:5]
- Rambam says a non-Jew who keeps a day of rest as a Sabbath is "obligated to die" in principle, though a court only punishes and warns. This is a direct problem for an SDA who keeps Saturday as a religious obligation. [Mishneh Torah, Kings and Wars 10:9]
- Becoming a Noahide means formally accepting the seven commandments, and Rambam says this is done before three Torah scholars. It is not a casual label, so don't pressure her toward it. [Mishneh Torah, Kings and Wars 8:10]
- Many authorities hold that Noahides must reject all idolatry. Trinitarian belief is debated, and many rabbis treat it as problematic for Noahides.
- Shared life goals, honesty and her free choice matter more than a conversion project.

## What the sources say

**Marriage and the Noahide laws.** Rambam lists six forbidden relations for a Noahide: his mother, his father's wife, a married woman, his maternal sister, a male, and an animal. He derives them from Genesis 2:24, "a man shall… cling to his wife" [Mishneh Torah, Kings and Wars 9:5]. A partner from another religion isn't on that list, so you don't face a halachic prohibition on this point. Questions about what counts as a valid Noahide marriage and divorce are more technical, and you should take them to a rabbi who knows Noahide law.

**Sabbath.** Rambam writes: "a gentile who rests, even on a weekday, observing that day as a Sabbath, is obligated to die… They are not to be allowed to originate a new religion or create mitzvot for themselves." A Jewish court would only beat or punish such a person and inform him of the liability. It would not execute him. He gives two options: either "become righteous converts and accept all the mitzvot," or "retain their statutes without adding or detracting" [Mishneh Torah, Kings and Wars 10:9]. Many modern Noahide teachers soften this. They say a non-Jew may rest on any day for ordinary reasons but should not treat it as a commanded Sabbath. Either way, this is a serious issue for an SDA, since keeping the Sabbath is central to her identity and her community.

**Torah study.** Rambam also says a non-Jew should not study Torah beyond the seven commandments [Mishneh Torah, Kings and Wars 10:9]. Later authorities discuss how far this goes. Many allow study of the Noahide laws and of Tanakh in a way that supports them. This matters if you plan to study together as a couple.

**Acceptance of the commandments.** Rambam describes the "resident alien" (*ger toshav*) as someone who accepts the seven commandments before three Torah scholars [Mishneh Torah, Kings and Wars 8:10]. He also says non-Jews are not forced to take on Torah and mitzvot. They are encouraged to keep the Noahide laws.

**Beliefs.** I'm giving this from memory, not from a source I looked up here. Many halachic authorities, including some who allow a Trinitarian "association" of other beings with God for non-Jews, still consider it a serious concern. Mainstream Noahide guidance generally asks you to reject worship of Jesus. Adventist doctrine also includes things like Ellen White's writings and the heavenly sanctuary teaching, which would need examination. Ask your rabbi for guidance on exactly where the line falls.

## Practical suggestions
- **Be honest early.** Tell her plainly what you believe and why. Show her the sources instead of just asking her to adopt a label.
- **Let her choose freely.** If she converts only to keep the relationship, it will probably be unstable and won't be real faith. Marry her as she is, or be prepared to find out you can't.
- **Decide how you'll live together before marriage.** Think about Sabbath, worship, holidays, food, and how you would raise children.
- **Find a rabbi.** Look for one who works with Noahides, such as through Noahide communities or Torah organizations. This area has disagreements among authorities, and your situation needs personal guidance.

I can look up more on the Trinity question, or on Noahide marriage, if you'd like.

answer:
**Short answer:** In Jewish sources, the ultimate Redeemer (*Go'el*) is God. He redeems Israel from Egypt and from every later exile, and he redeems individuals from distress. The same word also describes a human "kinsman-redeemer" with a legal duty to a relative, and the future human redeemer, the Messiah, who is God's agent. You didn't say which sense you mean, so I cover all three.

## Key Takeaways
- *Go'el* means "redeemer": someone who buys back, rescues, or restores.
- Legally, the *go'el* is the nearest relative who redeems a family member's land or freedom [Leviticus 25:25].
- Theologically, God is the Redeemer of Israel and of the individual.
- The Messiah, in Jewish thought, is a human king and God's agent of the final redemption. He is not God himself.
- The word is also used for personal rescue, as in Jacob's blessing and Job's cry.

## 1. The kinsman-redeemer (plain meaning)
The Torah says: "וּבָא גֹאֲלוֹ הַקָּרֹב אֵלָיו וְגָאַל אֵת מִמְכַּר אָחִיו". In the JPS translation: "the nearest redeemer shall come and redeem what that relative has sold" [Leviticus 25:25]. The *go'el* is the closest relative, and his duty is to keep land and family members from being lost. The Book of Ruth builds on this role, which is why Boaz is called a *go'el*.

## 2. God as Redeemer
The Tanakh uses the same word for God, who acts as Israel's closest kin and rescues them. The same applies to the individual. Jacob says: "הַמַּלְאָךְ הַגֹּאֵל אֹתִי מִכָּל רָע", "The Angel who has redeemed me from all harm" [Genesis 48:16]. Job says: "וַאֲנִי יָדַעְתִּי גֹּאֲלִי חָי", "But I know that my Vindicator lives" [Job 19:25]. His redeemer is the living God, who will vindicate him even in suffering.

Isaiah also speaks of a "Redeemer who will come to Zion" (Isaiah 59:20). I couldn't retrieve that text just now, so I'm citing it from memory and you should check it.

## 3. The Messiah and the future redemption
Rambam describes the Messiah as a human king from David's line. He will gather the exiles and restore Torah observance. He is not divine. Rambam sets this out in *Mishneh Torah, Kings and Wars* 11–12, and it is part of his Thirteen Principles of faith. I didn't retrieve those chapters in this answer. Redemption always comes from God, and the Messiah is his instrument.

If you meant something else, tell me and I'll go further. For example, you might mean the Redeemer in the Book of Ruth, the *Go'el HaDam* (blood avenger), or the line in the *Amidah* blessing "Go'el Yisrael." If you meant how other religions use the term, I can describe the Jewish understanding of the term and how it differs from theirs.

answer:
**Short answer:** No, it isn't an absolute ban. The Mishnah restricts one kind of inquiry: speculating about what existed *before* creation. Studying the creation account as it appears in the Torah is allowed, though it is meant to be done carefully and, ideally, with a teacher. Questions about pre-Adam creatures fall mostly under the second category, not the first.

## Key Takeaways
- The Mishnah warns against asking "what is above, what is below, what came before, what comes after" [Chagigah 11b].
- The Gemara reads this as a ban on speculating about what preceded creation. It does not ban studying the six days of creation.
- *Ma'aseh Bereshit* (the account of creation) may not be taught to two or more people together. It may be studied one-on-one, with a wise student.
- Ramban says the deeper meaning of creation is a received tradition, a "deep mystery" that can't be fully understood from the verses alone.
- Orthodox thinkers differ on pre-Adam beings and the age of the world, so this is an open area, not a settled one.

## The sources

**The Mishnah.** It says: "וְלֹא בְּמַעֲשֵׂה בְרֵאשִׁית בִּשְׁנַיִם… כׇּל הַמִּסְתַּכֵּל בְּאַרְבָּעָה דְּבָרִים, רָתוּי לוֹ כְּאִילּוּ לֹא בָּא לָעוֹלָם: מָה לְמַעְלָה, מָה לְמַטָּה, מָה לְפָנִים, וּמָה לְאָחוֹר."
Translation: "Nor [may one expound] the act of Creation before two… Whoever looks at four matters, it would have been better had he never entered the world: what is above, what is below, what came before, and what comes after." [Chagigah 11b]

**The Gemara's derivation.** It learns the limits from Deuteronomy 4:32, "כִּי שְׁאַל נָא לְיָמִים רִאשֹׁנִים":
- You may *not* ask about the time "before the world was created." The verse says "from the day God created man on the earth."
- You *may* ask about the six days of creation: "the first days that were before you."
- You may ask "from one end of heaven to the other," but not "what is above, what is below, what is before, what is after."

So the Gemara's own text permits inquiry into the six days of creation. The prohibition is on asking about what existed before the world began, and on metaphysical speculation beyond it.

**Ramban's view.** Ramban says creation is "סוֹד עָמֹק, אֵינוֹ מוּבָן מִן הַמִּקְרָאוֹת" ("a deep mystery, not understood from the verses"). It is known only through a tradition going back to Moses, and "those who know it are obligated to conceal it." [Ramban on Genesis 1:1:1] This is why the verses alone won't settle questions about the world's earliest stages.

## Pre-Adam creatures specifically
- There is a midrashic tradition that God made worlds and destroyed them before this one (Bereshit Rabbah 3:7). I couldn't retrieve the text just now, so check it yourself before relying on it. Whether it is meant literally is debated.
- Some read Genesis 1 as describing earlier phases, or as allowing for a very old universe. Others reject this. I haven't retrieved a specific source for either side here, so I'm not attributing positions to named authorities.
- Because the Mishnah's warning is about speculating on what lay *before* creation, many hold that reading the text and comparing it with science is a different matter. Others are more cautious. This is a real disagreement.

## Practically
Learning the text and its commentators is fine. Be careful about confident speculation beyond what the sources say, and about teaching deeper creation topics to a group. If you want to go deeper, I'd suggest working through Ramban on Genesis 1 and Rashi on Genesis 1:1 with a teacher. For your own situation, consult your rabbi.

If you tell me what you want to research (science and Genesis, the midrashim on earlier worlds, or the identity of the "pre-Adam" beings), I can look at specific sources with you.

answer:
I'm sorry you're carrying this. It sounds heavy. I may be misreading parts of your message, so correct me if I am. I'm taking it to mean that you looked at disturbing things, that you think you crossed a line into something like *avodah zarah* (idolatry), and that you asked God three times to get into yeshiva and didn't. Now you wonder why He would listen to you.

**Short answer:** In Jewish thought, God's willingness to listen doesn't depend on a clean record or on past prayers being answered. It depends on sincerity, and you're showing that now. A "no" to a request is also not proof that He isn't listening.

## Key Takeaways
- God is close to anyone who calls sincerely, not only to people who have done everything right.
- Torah says God wants you to return and live, not to be stuck in guilt.
- A prayer that wasn't answered the way you hoped isn't a rejection.
- Feeling broken is not a barrier. The verses describe it as the place where God is close.
- The practical next step is to talk to a rabbi or mentor, because this is hard to carry alone.

## Why He listens
- **Sincerity is the requirement.** "קָרוֹב יְהוָה לְכָל־קֹרְאָיו, לְכֹל אֲשֶׁר יִקְרָאֻהוּ בֶאֱמֶת" ("God is near to all who call, to all who call with sincerity") [Psalms 145:18]. The verse says *all*, and the only condition is that the call be real.
- **He wants your return.** "הֶחָפֹץ אֶחְפֹּץ מוֹת רָשָׁע... הֲלוֹא בְּשׁוּבוֹ מִדְּרָכָיו וְחָיָה" ("Is it my desire that the wicked shall die? … It is rather that they shall turn back from their ways and live") [Ezekiel 18:23]. Even if your past actions were as bad as you fear, the verse says God's desire is your *teshuvah* (repentance), not your punishment.
- **Pain doesn't disqualify you.** "קָרוֹב יְהוָה לְנִשְׁבְּרֵי־לֵב, וְאֶת־דַּכְּאֵי־רוּחַ יוֹשִׁיעַ" ("God is close to the brokenhearted; those crushed in spirit are delivered") [Psalms 34:19]. The distress you feel is not evidence against you.

## On the yeshiva requests
I haven't pulled a specific source for this part, so I'm giving a general idea from the tradition. A "no," or a "not yet," isn't the same as God not hearing you. Often we can't see why a door stays closed, and it doesn't mean your *teshuvah* or your wish to learn counts for nothing. Your desire to learn Torah is already valuable. You can learn now, with a *chavruta* (study partner), a local rabbi, or online, while the yeshiva question works itself out. Some yeshivot also have programs for people who come with a complicated past. A rabbi who knows you can help you find the right one.

## On what you did
I don't know exactly what you saw or did. A rabbi could help you sort out what is actually a serious violation and what is guilt that has grown larger than the facts. Most of us can't judge that well alone, especially when we feel ashamed.

Either way, the Torah's response to wrongdoing is *teshuvah*. It means regretting it, stopping, and resolving not to repeat it. That is a path, not a one-time verdict. People can start it at any point, including now.

## What you could do this week
- Say a short prayer in your own words, such as "I'm here, I made mistakes, please help me start again."
- Talk to a rabbi or mentor you trust about what happened. You don't have to give every detail.
- Set one small, steady learning habit, like ten minutes a day of Psalms or *Mishnah*.

If the guilt ever starts to feel like hopelessness, or you have thoughts of hurting yourself, please reach out now to someone you trust or to local emergency services. Please don't wait on that.

If you'd like, tell me more about what happened and what you're hoping for. I can help you find sources or think through next steps, though your own rabbi should guide you on the specifics.

I couldn't retrieve texts from Sefaria just now. The lookups failed, so none of what follows is verified against the text. I'm giving authors and works from memory, without page or section numbers. Please check each one before quoting it.

The three closest matches are Rabbi Eliyahu Dessler, Rav Shlomo Wolbe and Rabbi Jonathan Sacks. All three are modern, but none is a living rav. I can't responsibly attribute a specific passage to a living rabbi without checking it.

## Key Takeaways
- Rav Dessler's *Michtav MeEliyahu* ties the *bechira* (free choice) struggle to the shift from "taking" to "giving."
- Rav Wolbe's *Alei Shur* treats *ta'avah* (craving) as a force that grows when fed and that must be shaped by self-knowledge.
- Rabbi Sacks wrote on the tenth commandment, *lo tachmod* (do not covet), and on desire that comes from comparing ourselves to others.
- The classical root is Kohelet's "he who loves money will not be satisfied with money" [Ecclesiastes 5:9]. The midrash also says no one dies with half his desires fulfilled.

## The three sources

**1. Rabbi Eliyahu Dessler (d. 1954), *Michtav MeEliyahu*.**
- Look at his essays on *chesed* (giving) and on the "point of *bechira*."
- His theme is that the self is by nature oriented toward getting more, and that real choice begins where you push against that pull.
- Rav Dessler holds that *bechira* operates only at the edge of one's current level, so craving is the field on which choice is exercised.
- He also defines love through giving rather than taking.
- Some of his ideas are cited under his name but come from students' summaries, so check which volume you are quoting.

**2. Rav Shlomo Wolbe (d. 2005), *Alei Shur*.**
- This is a mussar work on self-building.
- He discusses desires and the inner drive for satisfaction.
- His approach is to know your inner life and work on it gradually, not to suppress it.
- I'm confident the theme is there, but I can't name the exact chapter.

**3. Rabbi Jonathan Sacks (d. 2020), *Covenant & Conversation*.**
- Look at his essays on *Yitro* (Exodus 20) about *lo tachmod*.
- The point I recall is that the Torah legislates even desire, which is unusual for a legal code.
- He links this to wanting what others have, which makes appetite endless because it is fed by comparison.
- I believe he draws on René Girard's idea of mimetic desire there, but check this.

## The classical roots they build on
- [Ecclesiastes 5:9]: "אֹהֵב כֶּסֶף לֹא יִשְׂבַּע כֶּסֶף" ("He who loves money will not be satisfied with money").
- Kohelet Rabbah, in a teaching I recall at 1:13, says "אין אדם מת וחצי תאותו בידו" (no one dies with half his desire in hand). I couldn't retrieve it to confirm the reference or wording.

If you want living voices, I can try the lookups again for Rabbi Akiva Tatz or others. I'd rather confirm the text than guess.

answer:
Reintento con las fuentes.Sucot es la fiesta de siete días, del 15 al 21 de Tishrei, en la que la Torá manda vivir en una *sucá* (cabaña) y tomar las Cuatro Especies. Recuerda la protección divina en el desierto y es "la época de nuestra alegría". Hoy es 23 de noviembre de 2026, así que la próxima Sucot empieza el 15 de Tishrei de 5788, que según Hebcal es el 16 de octubre de 2027.

Algunas consultas a Sefaria fallaron por límite de peticiones. Por eso los versículos del Levítico y el Shulján Aruj los resumo sin citarlos textualmente. Las fuentes que sí pude leer están citadas entre corchetes.

## Puntos clave

- Sucot cae el 15 de Tishrei y dura siete días, seguidos de Shemini Atzeret y Simjat Torá.
- Hay dos mitzvot centrales: habitar en la sucá y tomar las Cuatro Especies (*lulav*, *etrog*, *hadasim* y *aravot*).
- La sucá simboliza la fragilidad y la confianza en Dios: salimos de la vivienda fija y entramos en una vivienda temporal.
- Hay costumbres distintas entre las comunidades, como el *etrog* de Calabria o de Marruecos, el orden de las *hoshanot* y el ushpizin.
- Las leyes prácticas tienen muchos detalles. Conviene consultar a un rabino para cada caso.

## 1. Fuente y significado (pshat)

La Torá ordena en Levítico 23:33-43 la fiesta de siete días y la mitzvá de habitar en sucot. La razón que da es: "para que sepan sus generaciones que en sucot hice habitar a los hijos de Israel al sacarlos de Egipto" (Levítico 23:43). Ese versículo aparece citado en [Sukkah 2a](https://www.sefaria.org/Sukkah.2a).

El Talmud discute allí qué son esas *sucot*. En el mismo lugar, Rabá deriva de ese versículo que la sucá debe permitir "saber" que uno vive en ella. Por eso una sucá de más de 20 codos es inválida, ya que el ojo no percibe el techo.

Rabá también deriva de "en sucot habitarán siete días" una idea de fondo. La Torá dice: "durante siete días sal de una vivienda permanente y habita en una vivienda temporal" (*dirat arai*). Es decir, la sucá es una casa provisoria y no un lujo.

## 2. Las leyes básicas de la sucá

La Mishná [Sukkah 2a](https://www.sefaria.org/Sukkah.2a) establece que es inválida la sucá que:

- tiene un techo de más de 20 codos de altura (Rabí Yehudá la valida);
- mide menos de 10 *tefajim* de alto;
- no tiene tres paredes;
- tiene más sol que sombra bajo el techo.

El techo (*sejaj*) debe ser de material que crece de la tierra y está desprendido de ella. Esto lo sé de la tradición, pero no pude verificarlo ahora en las fuentes.

## 3. ¿Quién está obligado?

Según el Rambam, las mujeres, los esclavos y los menores están exentos de la sucá. El niño que ya no depende de su madre (cinco o seis años) está obligado por decreto rabínico, para educarlo en las mitzvot. Así lo dice [Mishneh Torah, Shofar, Sukkah and Lulav 6:1](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishneh_Torah,_Shofar,_Sukkah_and_Lulav.6.1).

Las mujeres están exentas porque es una mitzvá positiva atada al tiempo. Aun así, en muchas comunidades la cumplen voluntariamente.

## 4. Las Cuatro Especies

Según Levítico 23:40, se toman el fruto del árbol hermoso (*etrog*), las ramas de palmera (*lulav*), la rama del árbol frondoso (*hadas*, mirto) y los sauces del arroyo (*aravá*). Se agitan hacia las seis direcciones durante el *Halel*, tras bendecir "al netilat lulav". Este es el uso general de la tradición, pero no lo verifiqué aquí.

## 5. Estructura de la fiesta

- **Primer día (y segundo en la diáspora):** *Yom Tov*, con trabajo prohibido como en Shabat, salvo preparar comida.
- **Jol HaMoed:** los días intermedios. Hay *Halel*, *musaf* de la fiesta y *hoshanot*, que son vueltas alrededor de la *bimá* con las especies.
- **Hoshaná Rabá:** el séptimo día. Se dan siete vueltas y se golpean cinco ramas de *aravá*.
- **Shemini Atzeret:** el día 22, una fiesta aparte, con la oración por la lluvia (*Geshem*).
- **Simjat Torá:** en la diáspora, el día 23, cuando se termina y se reinicia el ciclo de lectura de la Torá. En Israel coincide con Shemini Atzeret.

En Shemini Atzeret, en la diáspora, se come en la sucá sin bendición, según la mayoría de las comunidades. En Israel las costumbres varían.

## 6. Diferencias entre comunidades

- **Asquenazíes:** siguen al Rema. Algunos tienen la costumbre de dormir en la sucá, y otros se excusan en climas fríos o lluviosos.
- **Sefardíes:** siguen al Shulján Aruj y a Rav Ovadia Yosef. Rav Ovadia sostiene que se debe dormir en la sucá.
- **Jabad:** la costumbre es no comer ni beber nada fuera de la sucá. Esto incluye el agua, aunque no se exige tanto en cantidades pequeñas. Además, Jabad no practica el *ushpizin* como los demás, sino con una lectura propia.
- **Calendario:** en Israel hay un solo día de Yom Tov al principio, y en la diáspora hay dos.

Estas costumbres las conozco de la tradición, sin haberlas verificado ahora en los textos. Si necesitas una ley exacta, dime tu comunidad y la reviso con fuentes.

## 7. Temas más profundos (no pshat)

- **Las nubes de gloria:** según una opinión talmúdica, las *sucot* son las nubes que rodearon a Israel en el desierto. Otra opinión dice que son cabañas reales.
- **Los 70 toros:** según la tradición, se ofrecían 70 toros por las 70 naciones (Números 29). Hoy vemos en ello el aspecto universal de Sucot.
- **Ushpizin:** es una costumbre cabalística. Cada noche se invita a un huésped espiritual: Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Moisés, Aarón, José y David.
- **Kohélet:** se lee en Sucot en la tradición asquenazí y en la sefardí. Habla de lo pasajero de las cosas y por eso encaja con la sucá.

## Para estudiar más

Si quieres, puedo profundizar en cualquiera de estos temas: las leyes detalladas de la sucá, las Cuatro Especies, Hoshaná Rabá, Shemini Atzeret y Simjat Torá, o un *dvar Torá*. Dime también tu comunidad (asquenazí, sefardí o Jabad) y la ley concreta que te interesa. Para cualquier caso práctico, consulta a tu rabino.

It cites SA 235:1 instead of 235:3, does not say that bedtime Shema fails to replace Maariv, and casts vague doubt on saying the blessings after midnight even though the Shulchan Arukh permits them until dawn.

answer:
I couldn't retrieve the texts just now because the Sefaria library is rate-limiting requests. The answer below is from my own knowledge, and I haven't checked the wording against the sources. Please confirm the references.

The Mishnah says the evening Shema may be recited until the end of the first watch of the night, and Rabban Gamliel says until dawn (*alot hashachar*). The halacha follows Rabban Gamliel, so the latest time is dawn. Lechatchila (ideally), one should recite it before *chatzot* (halachic midnight), as a safeguard.

## Key Takeaways
- The Mishnah's first view is until the end of the first third of the night, and Rabban Gamliel says until dawn.
- The halacha follows Rabban Gamliel: the evening Shema is valid until *alot hashachar* (dawn).
- The Sages told people to finish by *chatzot* (midnight) as a fence, to keep them from neglecting the mitzvah.
- Therefore, ideally say it before midnight. Bedieved (after the fact), it counts until dawn.
- Ashkenazim and Sephardim agree on this in principle. Practical details differ.

## The sources (not retrieved; please verify)
- [Mishnah Berakhot 1:1] sets the deadline. The Sages say "until midnight" (*chatzot*), and Rabban Gamliel says "until the dawn rises."
- [Berakhot 8b] and the following pages bring the Gemara's discussion of the Sages' "fence." It explains that their "until midnight" ruling is a safeguard, and that the mitzvah itself runs until dawn.
- [Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chayim 235:1] and [Mishneh Torah, Reading the Shema 1:9] rule that the time runs until dawn. I believe they also say that one should ideally finish by midnight, but I haven't confirmed the wording.

## Practical points
- **Chatzot** is the midpoint of the night. It falls about halfway between sunset and sunrise, or between nightfall and dawn, depending on the opinion. Check a local zmanim table for your city.
- **Dawn** (*alot hashachar*) is about 72 minutes before sunrise by the common calculation, though opinions differ.
- If you reach midnight without having said it, say it anyway. It counts, and you don't lose the mitzvah.
- Some authorities discuss whether to say the blessings with the Shema after midnight. For this the practice is to consult a rabbi, since opinions differ.
- Many people also say the verses of Shema again (or the Shema on the bed) at bedtime. That is a separate custom.

I can give you today's *chatzot* and *alot hashachar* if you tell me your city. I can also try again to fetch the texts above.

Consult your rabbi for your own situation.

answer:
**Short answer:** Birkat HaChama isn't tied to the sun's actual astronomical position. It's tied to the calculation of Shmuel, which Chazal and the Shulchan Arukh adopted. In that calculation the solar year is exactly 365¼ days. Over 28 years this gives a whole number of weeks, so the sun returns to the same weekday and hour. Poskim have consistently followed this halachic convention and not corrected it to modern astronomy.

I could only retrieve [Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chayim 229:2] before the library started rate-limiting me. The Gemara and Rishonim below are from memory and I haven't verified them. Please check them before relying on them.

## Key Takeaways
- The Shulchan Arukh defines the blessing by Shmuel's cycle: every 28 years, when the tekufah begins at the start of the night before Wednesday.
- Shmuel's year (365¼ days) is slightly longer than the true solar year (about 365.2422 days).
- The mismatch is known. Today the "halachic" tekufah falls about 2½ weeks after the actual spring equinox.
- Chazal themselves knew of a more precise figure (Rav Adda's) and still used Shmuel's for this blessing.
- The blessing marks a traditional cycle of creation, so it follows the sages' fixed calculation. It doesn't follow a measurement.

## The source and the math
The ruling is in [Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chayim 229:2]. It reads: "הרואה חמה בתקופתה והוא מכ״ח לכ״ח שנה והתקופה בתחלת ליל ד׳ כשרואה אותה ביום ד׳ בבקר אומר ברוך עושה בראשית." In translation: "One who sees the sun at its tekufah, which occurs every 28 years, with the tekufah beginning at the start of the night before Wednesday, says on Wednesday morning: 'Blessed… Who makes the works of creation.'"

The basis is the Gemara in Berakhot 59b, which I haven't been able to retrieve. As I recall it, the sun was created on the fourth day (Wednesday), and the cycle is the sun's return to its position at creation.

Here is why the cycle is 28 years:
- Shmuel's year is 365¼ days.
- 28 × 365¼ = 10,227 days, which is exactly 1,461 weeks.
- After 28 years the tekufah therefore returns to the same weekday and hour.
- In Shmuel's reckoning, that hour is the start of Tuesday night, so the blessing falls on Wednesday morning.

## The astronomical discrepancy
- The true tropical year is about 365.2422 days. Shmuel's is about 11 minutes longer per year, which adds up to roughly one day per 128–130 years.
- Shmuel's year is the same as the Julian calendar's. In our era, "Nisan tekufah" therefore falls around April 8 on the civil calendar, though the real equinox is around March 20. The last Birkat HaChama was in April 2009, and the next is expected April 8, 2037. That is Erev Pesach, but please check with a calendar.
- Even on its own terms the 28-year cycle isn't perfect. A true astronomical return to the same weekday and hour would take much longer.

## Why we still follow the 28-year cycle
These are my own explanations, and I haven't verified them against specific authorities.

1. **The Gemara and the codes define the mitzvah by Shmuel's tekufah, not by observation.** The blessing is a halachic category. Halacha often uses fixed conventions that don't match astronomical reality. The Hebrew calendar's molad is one example.
2. **Chazal knew of other calculations.** Rav Adda's tekufah is more precise. The Rambam uses it in the laws of the calendar. Even so, the blessing was never moved to Rav Adda's figure. That shows the blessing isn't meant as a measurement.
3. **The blessing is about creation and tradition.** Its text, *oseh ma'aseh bereshit*, praises God for creation. The cycle is a reminder that the sun has returned to the position of its creation. It's a commemorative framework, so a divergence of days from the actual equinox doesn't invalidate it.
4. **Changing the practice would undo a universal custom.** Practice has stayed with the Gemara and the Shulchan Arukh. I'm not aware of any mainstream posek who moved the date to the astronomical equinox. I haven't verified every opinion, so a rav can tell you whether any authority discusses this.

## Practical note
Follow the community date, which is the Wednesday morning after the Shmuel tekufah. In [Mishnah Berurah 229:5], one should look at the sun long enough to bless but not stare at it. Looking too long dims the eyes, citing Chagigah 16. For questions about timing, such as weather or arriving late, consult your rabbi.
