answer:
**Salmo 90 (Tehilim 90)** es la única "plegaria de Moisés" del Salterio. Contrasta la eternidad de Dios con la fragilidad del ser humano, y termina pidiendo sabiduría, compasión y que nuestras obras tengan sentido. Sefaria no tenía traducción al español, así que la traducción que sigue es mía, hecha a partir del hebreo y de la versión inglesa de Sefaria. La cito como [Psalms 90:1-17].

## Puntos clave
- Moisés presenta a Dios como "refugio" eterno, anterior a la creación.
- La vida humana es breve como la hierba, y está marcada por el pecado y el sufrimiento.
- El centro del salmo es el versículo 12: aprender a "contar nuestros días" para adquirir un corazón sabio.
- El salmo pide el regreso de la compasión divina y alegría proporcional a los años de aflicción.
- Termina pidiendo que Dios afirme "la obra de nuestras manos".

## Texto (traducción propia)

1. Plegaria de Moisés, hombre de Dios. Señor, tú has sido para nosotros refugio de generación en generación.
2. Antes de que nacieran los montes, y de que formaras la tierra y el mundo, de eternidad a eternidad tú eres Dios.
3. Haces volver al hombre al polvo, y dices: "Volved, hijos de Adán".
4. Pues mil años ante tus ojos son como el día de ayer que pasó, como una vigilia de la noche.
5. Los arrebatas como un sueño; por la mañana son como la hierba que se renueva.
6. Por la mañana florece y se renueva; por la tarde se marchita y se seca.
7. Pues nos consumimos por tu ira, y por tu furor quedamos aterrados.
8. Pusiste nuestras iniquidades delante de ti, nuestros pecados ocultos a la luz de tu rostro.
9. Pues todos nuestros días declinan bajo tu enojo; acabamos nuestros años como un suspiro.
10. Los días de nuestros años son setenta años, y si por fortaleza llegan a ochenta, su orgullo es fatiga y vanidad, porque pasan pronto y volamos.
11. ¿Quién conoce la fuerza de tu ira? Tu furor es tan grande como el temor que se te debe.
12. Enséñanos a contar nuestros días, para que alcancemos un corazón sabio.
13. Vuelve, Señor. ¿Hasta cuándo? Compadécete de tus siervos.
14. Sácianos por la mañana con tu bondad, y cantaremos y nos alegraremos todos nuestros días.
15. Alégranos tantos días como nos afligiste, tantos años como vimos el mal.
16. Que se manifieste tu obra a tus siervos, y tu esplendor sobre sus hijos.
17. Que la gracia del Señor, nuestro Dios, esté sobre nosotros; la obra de nuestras manos confírmala sobre nosotros, y la obra de nuestras manos confírmala.

## Estructura (explicación mía)
- **Versículos 1–2:** Dios es eterno y es el hogar (*maón*) de Israel a lo largo de las generaciones.
- **Versículos 3–6:** el ser humano es mortal. "Mil años son como ayer" [Psalms 90:4] expresa la distancia entre el tiempo de Dios y el nuestro.
- **Versículos 7–11:** la brevedad de la vida se relaciona con el pecado y con la ira divina. "Setenta años" [Psalms 90:10] es la medida típica de la vida.
- **Versículos 12–17:** es la parte de la súplica. Se pide sabiduría, el regreso de la compasión y alegría que equilibre el sufrimiento.

## Notas
- "Hombre de Dios" es un título de Moisés. El salmo se atribuye a él, aunque no he consultado aquí los comentarios clásicos sobre la autoría o la época.
- Algunos términos son difíciles. Por ejemplo, *dakká* ("polvo", v. 3) y *kemó hegué* ("como un suspiro", v. 9) tienen varias traducciones posibles.
- Tradicionalmente este salmo se recita en Shabat por la mañana (*Pesukei DeZimra*) y también al comienzo del Salmo 91 en el rezo vespertino de la salida de Shabat. No lo he verificado en las fuentes durante esta consulta.

Si quieres, puedo añadir lo que dicen Rashi, Ibn Ezra o Radak sobre versículos concretos, por ejemplo el 4 o el 12.

El Salmo 150 es el último del libro de Salmos. Es una invitación a que todo lo que respira alabe a Dios, con todos los instrumentos musicales. Es una conclusión de alabanza a todo el libro.

## Puntos clave
- Dios es alabado en su santuario y en el firmamento.
- Se alaba por sus hazañas y por su grandeza.
- Se enumeran instrumentos: *shofar*, arpa, lira, pandero, flauta, címbalos.
- El versículo final dice que toda alma (*neshamá*) debe alabar a Dios.

## Texto y traducción (mía)

1. הַלְלוּ־יָהּ הַֽלְלוּ־אֵל בְּקָדְשׁוֹ הַֽלְלֽוּהוּ בִּרְקִיעַ עֻזּוֹ
 *¡Aleluya! Alaben a Dios en su santuario; alábenlo en el firmamento de su poder.*

2. הַֽלְלֽוּהוּ בִּגְבוּרֹתָיו הַֽלְלֽוּהוּ כְּרֹב גֻּדְלוֹ
 *Alábenlo por sus proezas; alábenlo según la abundancia de su grandeza.*

3. הַֽלְלֽוּהוּ בְּתֵקַע שׁוֹפָר הַֽלְלֽוּהוּ בְּנֵבֶל וְכִנּוֹר
 *Alábenlo con el sonido del *shofar*; alábenlo con arpa y lira.*

4. הַֽלְלֽוּהוּ בְּתֹף וּמָחוֹל הַֽלְלֽוּהוּ בְּמִנִּים וְעֻגָב
 *Alábenlo con pandero y danza; alábenlo con instrumentos de cuerda y flauta.*

5. הַֽלְלֽוּהוּ בְצִלְצְלֵי־שָׁמַע הַֽלְלֽוּהוּ בְּצִלְצְלֵי תְרוּעָה
 *Alábenlo con címbalos sonoros; alábenlo con címbalos resonantes.*

6. כֹּל הַנְּשָׁמָה תְּהַלֵּל יָהּ הַֽלְלוּ־יָהּ
 *Todo lo que tiene aliento alabe a Dios. ¡Aleluya!*

## Comentario breve
- **Estructura:** el verbo "alabar" (*halelu*) aparece trece veces en el salmo, según lo recuerdo. No lo verifiqué en este momento. Los versículos responden a tres preguntas: dónde se alaba (v. 1), por qué (v. 2) y con qué (vv. 3–5).
- **Último versículo:** el Midrash lo lee así: "todo aliento (*neshamá*)" alabe a Dios. Cada respiración es una ocasión de alabanza. No pude recuperar la cita exacta, así que no la doy.
- **Uso litúrgico:** el salmo se recita en *Pesukei DeZimrá*, la parte de alabanzas de la oración de la mañana (*Shajarit*). Allí cierra la serie de salmos de "Aleluya".

Si quieres, vuelvo a consultar Sefaria para traerte el texto verificado y comentarios como el de Rashi o Radak.

answer:
The sources I could check don't show any mainstream authority who removes tefillin during Hallel. The standard practice is the reverse. I couldn't confirm the view you're asking about, so I'd rather tell you that than guess a name.

## Key Takeaways
- In the Shulchan Arukh, tefillin are normally kept on until after *Uva LeTziyon*, and on Rosh Chodesh they come off before Musaf.
- Hallel on Rosh Chodesh and Chol HaMoed comes earlier in the service, so tefillin are worn through it.
- I found no source that has tefillin removed mid-Hallel. Searches for one failed because of a tool error, so I can't rule out a minority custom.

## What the sources say
The Shulchan Arukh rules: "נהגו העולם שלא לחלוץ תפילין עד אחר קדושת ובא לציון" ("The widespread custom is not to remove tefillin until after the Kedushah of *Uva LeTziyon*") [Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chayim 25:13]. It adds a Kabbalistic view that they stay on until after three *Kedushot* and four *Kaddishim*. It also says: "וביום ראש חודש חולצים אותם קודם תפלת מוסף" ("On Rosh Chodesh we remove them before Musaf").

The Rema extends this to Chol HaMoed. He notes that the custom everywhere is to remove them before Musaf.

The Mishnah Berurah gives the timing. On Rosh Chodesh, the *Eliyahu Rabba* says to remove them after *Uva LeTziyon* and before saying *Yehi Ratzon… sheNishmor Chukecha*. This avoids an interruption between Kaddish and the Amidah [Mishnah Berurah 25:59].

In all of these, the point of removal is Musaf, not Hallel.

## Possible things you may have heard about
I can't confirm any of these from what I retrieved:
- **Chol HaMoed.** Some communities don't wear tefillin at all on Chol HaMoed, so there is nothing to remove at Hallel. This is a separate dispute, and I haven't verified who holds which view.
- **Rosh Chodesh Hallel.** You may have heard of a local custom of removing tefillin before it.

If you tell me where you saw or heard this (a specific day, a community, or a book), I can look it up properly. If this is for practice, ask your rabbi what your community's custom is.

answer:
Rosh Hashanah suits a drasha on community because the day is itself built around the collective. The Torah reading, the shofar and the judgment all treat Israel as a single body. Below are sources I retrieved, grouped by theme with a suggested angle for each. I didn't find anything specific to Conservative movement sources, so these are classical texts that work in any pulpit.

## Key Takeaways
- The covenant text read just before Rosh Hashanah, [Deuteronomy 29:9-14], includes everyone, "from woodchopper to waterdrawer", and even those not present.
- Hillel's "do not separate yourself from the community" in [Pirkei Avot 2:4] is a good motto for the day.
- Rambam in [Mishneh Torah, Repentance 3:11] treats withdrawal from the community as a serious spiritual failing, even without any sin.
- The Talmud says communal judgment and communal repentance work differently from an individual's ([Rosh Hashanah 18a]).
- The shofar blower acts as a *shaliach tzibbur* (communal representative) who has the whole congregation in mind ([Rosh Hashanah 29a]).

## 1. A covenant of everyone: Deuteronomy 29
Nitzavim is read shortly before Rosh Hashanah, and it is a good opening text.

> "אַתֶּם נִצָּבִים הַיּוֹם כֻּלְּכֶם לִפְנֵי יְהֹוָה אֱלֹהֵיכֶם… טַפְּכֶם נְשֵׁיכֶם וְגֵרְךָ אֲשֶׁר בְּקֶרֶב מַחֲנֶיךָ, מֵחֹטֵב עֵצֶיךָ עַד שֹׁאֵב מֵימֶיךָ" [Deuteronomy 29:9-10]
> "You stand this day, all of you, before the ETERNAL your God: … your children, your wives, even the stranger within your camp, from woodchopper to waterdrawer."

- **Inclusion:** The list runs from leaders to laborers, and it includes the convert.
- **Across time:** Verse 14 says the covenant is made "with those who are standing here with us this day… and with those who are not with us here this day." The community includes the absent and future generations. You could apply this to the members who aren't in the room.
- **A way in:** Ask who is in our "camp" and who we would never think to name.

## 2. Hillel: "Do not separate yourself from the community"
> "הִלֵּל אוֹמֵר, אַל תִּפְרֹשׁ מִן הַצִּבּוּר, וְאַל תַּאֲמִין בְּעַצְמְךָ עַד יוֹם מוֹתְךָ, וְאַל תָּדִין אֶת חֲבֵרְךָ עַד שֶׁתַּגִּיעַ לִמְקוֹמוֹ" [Pirkei Avot 2:4]
> "Hillel said: do not separate yourself from the community; do not trust in yourself until the day of your death; do not judge your fellow until you have reached his place."

The three clauses are linked. Self-righteous isolation and harsh judgment of others go together, and on a day of self-judgment that is a useful point. The mishnah is my source here. The link I draw to Rosh Hashanah is my own.

## 3. Rambam: the cost of withdrawing
Rambam includes among those who forfeit a share in the world to come:

> "הַפּוֹרֵשׁ מִדַּרְכֵי צִבּוּר… וְאֵינוֹ עוֹשֶׂה מִצְוֹת בִּכְלָלָן וְלֹא נִכְנָס בְּצָרָתָן וְלֹא מִתְעַנֶּה בְּתַעֲנִיתָן" [Mishneh Torah, Repentance 3:11]
> "One who separates from the ways of the community… does not fulfill mitzvot together with them, does not take part in their hardships, or join in their fasts."

- **Not about sin:** Rambam says this applies "even though he has not transgressed any sins." The offense is being absent from communal life.
- **Practical test:** The three markers are doing mitzvot together, sharing in others' troubles, and joining communal observance. Each can become a question for the congregation.
- **Caution:** The language is severe. A congregation of mixed observance may hear it as exclusion, so frame it as a call to belong rather than a threat.

## 4. Judgment, individual and communal
The mishnah says all creatures "pass before Him like *benei maron*", and cites "He Who fashions their hearts alike" [Mishnah Rosh Hashanah 1:2], from Psalms 33:15. The verse's phrase *yachad libam*, "their hearts together", can be read as a statement about community.

The Gemara adds a distinction. Individuals should seek God "while He may be found" (Isaiah 55:6), which Rabbah bar Avuha places in the Ten Days of Repentance. For a community, the Gemara cites "as the Lord our God whenever we call upon Him" (Deuteronomy 4:7) and says a communal decree can be torn up even after it is sealed [Rosh Hashanah 18a]. The Gemara raises this as a difficulty and resolves it by distinguishing "individual" from "community."

Read plainly, a community has a different and wider access to mercy than any one person does. That gives you a message that we are stronger praying together than alone.

## 5. The shofar and the communal representative
The Gemara discusses someone who hears the shofar while passing the synagogue. It explains that this works because the blower is a *shaliach tzibbur* "whose intent is for the whole world" (*d'da'atei al kulei alma*). Rabbi Yose says an individual blower must have specific intent, but a communal representative need not [Rosh Hashanah 29a]. The same sugya says "everyone is obligated in the shofar", listing priests, Levites, Israelites, converts and freed slaves.

This can support a theme of a leader who carries everyone's obligation, and of people who each fulfill their duty through the other.

## 6. The sinners among us (a source I could not fully check)
The Talmud on [Keritot 6b] discusses the incense (*ketoret*). I recall the tradition that one of its ingredients, galbanum (*chelbenah*), smells bad yet is part of the sacred mixture. It is traditionally taken to mean that sinners belong in the community. Sefaria's text of that daf was truncated in my retrieval, so I could not read the passage and I'm not quoting it. Look it up before you use it. It is a strong image for an inclusive message.

## Possible structure
1. **Open** with Nitzavim: "from woodchopper to waterdrawer."
2. **Problem:** We are tempted to stand apart, either by pride or by disengagement ([Pirkei Avot 2:4]).
3. **Develop** the communal judgment of [Rosh Hashanah 18a] and the shofar blower of [Rosh Hashanah 29a].
4. **Challenge** with Rambam's three markers from [Mishneh Torah, Repentance 3:11], phrased as things to do this year.
5. **Close** with a concrete commitment, such as showing up for someone's *shiva*, joining a communal fast or program, or calling a member who has drifted away.

I can pull Rashi, Ramban or Sforno on Deuteronomy 29, or the Unetaneh Tokef text, if you'd like more.

Here is a source list for your kuntres. I could only retrieve a few texts before the Sefaria tool was rate-limited. I mark those as **[verified]**. The rest are well-known sources that I did not retrieve, so check the exact references and wording before printing. I have not guessed any se'if or daf numbers I wasn't sure of.

## Key Takeaways
- The core halacha is in [Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chayim 124], which requires silence and concentration during the *chazaras hashatz* (repetition of the Amidah).
- The Shulchan Arukh's strongest statement is that if nine people are not paying attention, the chazan's blessings are "almost in vain".
- The source for the repetition is the Talmud in Rosh Hashanah and Berakhot. It is a communal institution, not a break in the davening.
- A good chizuk kuntres can pair the halacha with the sources on the power of *amen*, so the reader learns what he gains and not only what he is forbidden to do.

## 1. Core halacha (verified)
- **[Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chayim 124:1]** The chazan repeats the Amidah so that anyone who cannot pray can fulfil his obligation by listening. That listener must concentrate from beginning to end, may not interrupt or converse, and takes three steps back at the end.
- **[Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chayim 124:4]** This is the key passage for your title.
  - The Hebrew reads: "כשש"צ חוזר התפלה הקהל יש להם לשתוק ולכוין לברכות שמברך החזן ולענות אמן."
  - Translation: when the chazan repeats the prayer, the congregation should be silent, focus on his blessings, and answer amen.
  - Next: "ואם אין ט' מכוונים לברכותיו קרוב להיות ברכותיו לבטלה", meaning that if nine are not focusing, his blessings are almost in vain.
  - Then: "לכן כל אדם יעשה עצמו כאילו אין ט' זולתו", so each person should act as if there were no nine others.
  - This works well as a chizuk theme: your attention counts toward the minyan.
  - The Hagahot Minhagim, quoted in the same se'if, records a custom that the whole congregation stands.

## 2. Sources to retrieve and check
**Talmud (the origin of the repetition)**
- **[Rosh Hashanah 34b]** The Gemara asks why the congregation prays and then the chazan prays again, and explains it as being for those who are not proficient. Read the sugya in full. The mishnah on that page was **[verified]** as being about shofar and blessings, so find the exact segment that discusses the repetition.
- **[Berakhot 21b]** The Talmud discusses the requirement of a minyan for *kedushah* and for answering. Check the exact lines.
- **[Sotah 39b]** This is a discussion of answering *amen*. Verify the details.
- **Shabbat 119b** discusses the great reward of answering amen with all one's strength. Verify the details.

**Rishonim and codes**
- **Rambam, Mishneh Torah, Laws of Prayer and the Priestly Blessing, chapter 9** covers the chazan's repetition. I could not retrieve it, so verify the halacha number.
- **Tur and Beit Yosef, Orach Chayim 124** are the background to the Shulchan Arukh.
- **Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chayim 125** covers amen after the blessings, and the other simanim near 124 cover the chazan's conduct.

**Later authorities for practice**
- **Mishnah Berurah 124**, in the Be'ur Halakhah and the se'ifim on talking during the repetition. Retrieve and read it.
- **Arukh HaShulchan, Orach Chayim 124.**
- **Kitzur Shulchan Arukh** on the laws of prayer.
- **Aruch HaShulchan and Mishnah Berurah** on which parts the congregation says along with the chazan. These include *Modim DeRabbanan* and *Kedushah*, and customs differ.
- **Chabad:** **Shulchan Aruch HaRav, Orach Chayim 124** covers the conduct. Chabad's customs on kedushah and on what is said aloud are worth checking.
- **Sephardi:** **Ben Ish Chai** and **Yalkut Yosef** on talking and learning during the repetition. Cite them only once you have the exact text.

## 3. Chizuk and thought sources (check each before printing)
- The Zohar and the *Sefer Chasidim* speak strongly about talking during prayer. I did not retrieve them, so verify before quoting.
- The statement that anyone who answers amen with all his strength has the gates of Gan Eden opened for him is from Shabbat 119b. Verify it.

6. Community differences, labeled Ashkenazi, Sephardi, and Chabad.

answer:
Yes, a parent may pray for a child, and Job is the model case. Praying for someone differs from taking over their responsibility. Prayer doesn't cancel the child's accountability. It asks God for help, guidance, and mercy, and it can give the child a better chance to choose well.

## Key Takeaways
- Individual responsibility is a firm principle: [Ezekiel 18:20] says a parent doesn't bear a child's guilt, and a child doesn't bear a parent's.
- Job's offerings in [Job 1:5] don't contradict this, because they ask for atonement and protection and don't claim to take the guilt.
- Job fears sins "in their hearts" (*bilvavam*), which no human court can see. Only God can address that, so prayer is the natural response.
- Scripture itself shows parents praying for children, and shows God's mercy responding to intercession.
- Praying for a child's thoughts doesn't remove free will. It asks for help in using it.

## The text
Here is [Job 1:5]: "כִּי אָמַר אִיּוֹב אוּלַי חָטְאוּ בָנַי וּבֵרְכוּ אֱלֹהִים בִּלְבָבָם". In the Sefaria translation: "for Job thought, 'Perhaps my children have sinned and blasphemed God in their thoughts.'"

Some details matter for your question:
- Job says "perhaps." He isn't claiming they sinned, and he isn't answering for them.
- *Vayekadshem* ("he sanctified them") means, per [Rashi on Job 1:5], that he "prepared them and summoned them." He didn't just pray over them. He called them to ready themselves, so they took part.
- Rashi also notes that *uverchu* ("blessed") is a euphemism for cursing God.
- The Hebrew *kakha ya'aseh Iyov kol hayamim* says this was his constant practice.

## Why this doesn't contradict individual responsibility
[Ezekiel 18:20] says: "הַנֶּפֶשׁ הַחֹטֵאת הִיא תָמוּת, בֵּן לֹא יִשָּׂא בַּעֲוֺן הָאָב". That verse is about judgment. It says God doesn't punish one person for another's guilt. Job isn't asking that his children be spared their own accountability. He is doing two other things, which are my reading of the verse:
1. **Asking for mercy.** The offering is a request for forgiveness for a possible lapse. Asking for mercy on someone's behalf doesn't deny that they're responsible.
2. **Taking responsibility for his own role.** A parent is responsible for educating and influencing. Praying for children is part of that duty, and it doesn't replace theirs.

## Other examples of praying for others
- Abraham prays for Sodom and for Avimelekh, and Moses prays for Israel after the Golden Calf. None of them denies that the people are responsible.
- The Torah's model of intercession assumes both things at once. People are accountable, and God can respond to prayer.
- Parents' blessings and prayers for children are a lasting Jewish custom. On Friday night, for example, parents bless their children.

I haven't checked specific sources for these other examples in this answer. I mention them as general background.

## Free will and prayer
Some readers worry that praying for someone's thoughts treats their mind as something God overrides. The usual view is different. In the Rambam's picture, free will is real, and prayer works within it. It can bring mercy, help, favorable circumstances, and a clearer mind. It doesn't force a result. Job's offerings can be read the same way. They don't guarantee what his children think. They show concern and ask God to help.

Job's case is also unusual, since the book itself questions how human righteousness and divine justice relate. So it makes sense to read his practice as a model of parental concern, and not as a ruling on the mechanics of reward and punishment.

If you'd like, I can look at how specific commentators (Ibn Ezra, Ralbag, Metzudat David) understand Job's motivation here.

answer:
Rosh Hashanah's central prayers are built from a few Talmudic ideas. The Amidah has three themes (Kingship, Remembrance, Shofar). The shofar is blown twice. We are judged as we are now. Several things can change a decree. Below are talking points with sources. I read the Rosh Hashanah passages in Sefaria, but the piyyutim and Avinu Malkeinu came from memory, and I mark those.

## Key Takeaways
- The Musaf Amidah is organized around *Malchuyot* (Kingship), *Zichronot* (Remembrance) and *Shofarot*, each with its own verses and blasts.
- The Talmud says we are judged by our deeds "at that hour", so a person can change course now.
- Three books are opened. Most of us are "in-between" and are held in suspense until Yom Kippur.
- A decree can be torn up by charity, outcry, a change of deeds, and (in the Talmud's list) a change of name or place. This is the background to the "teshuvah, tefillah, tzedakah" refrain of *Unetaneh Tokef*.
- Blowing the shofar a second time, while standing in the Amidah, is said to "confuse the Satan". It shows love of the mitzvah.

## 1. The three themes of Musaf: Malchuyot, Zichronot, Shofarot
**Source.** The Mishnah gives the order of the blessings: Avot, Gevurot and Kedushat HaShem, with Kingship included. Then come Kedushat HaYom, Zichronot and Shofarot, with shofar blasts after the last three. [Rosh Hashanah 32a]

The Gemara derives the three themes from Leviticus 23:24, "a solemn rest, a memorial of blasts, a sacred convocation" (*Shabbaton zichron teruah mikra kodesh*). In Rabbi Eliezer's reading, "*zikhron*" points to Zichronot and "*teruah*" to Shofarot. Malchuyot is learned from "I am the Lord your God" (*Ani Hashem Elokeichem*). [Rosh Hashanah 32a]

**Insight to share.** The three themes answer three questions:
- Malchuyot asks who is in charge.
- Zichronot asks whether God remembers us.
- Shofarot asks how we cry out, and how God calls to us.

The day begins with crowning God and only then asks for our own judgment. The Gemara also records a debate over whether Kingship gets its own shofar blasts, and over whether it gets ten verses. That shows how seriously the sages took the order. [Rosh Hashanah 32a]

*From memory, not retrieved here:* Rosh Hashanah 16a gives the well-known line in which God says to say Malchuyot, Zichronot and Shofarot so that He be our King and we be remembered, and the shofar is the means. It is worth reading aloud from the daf.

**Question for the room.** Why does a day of judgment open with coronation and not with a list of sins?

## 2. Why blow the shofar twice? "To confuse the Satan"
The Gemara asks why we blow again during the Amidah after the blasts before it. Its answer is "to confuse the Satan" (*learbev et ha-Satan*). Rabbi Yitzchak adds that a year in which the shofar is not sounded at its start will see "*meri'in*" (a pun on blowing and on misfortune) at its end. [Rosh Hashanah 16b]

**Insight.** In the Gemara's own reading, the double blowing shows Israel's love for the mitzvah, and that is what disarms the accuser. This is a *drash* (homiletical reading), not a literal claim about a being. You can present it as the idea that eagerness for a mitzvah changes how we are seen. It is a more hopeful picture than "God is looking for our flaws".

## 3. You are judged as you are now
Rabbi Yitzchak says a person is judged only by their deeds "at that hour". The proof is Ishmael, whom God heard "where he is" (*ba'asher hu sham*), whatever his descendants would later do. [Rosh Hashanah 16b]

**Insight.** This is the legal basis for the hope of teshuvah. The present moment counts, and sincerity in the shofar service and the Amidah is not a formality.

The same passage says three books are opened on Rosh Hashanah, for the wholly righteous, the wholly wicked and the in-between. The in-between "are suspended from Rosh Hashanah until Yom Kippur". If they merit it they are written for life, and if not, for death. [Rosh Hashanah 16b]

This explains why the Ten Days of Repentance exist. Most of us are the *beinonim*, so the balance is still open and our choices matter now.

## 4. "Teshuvah, tefillah, tzedakah": what tears up a decree
Rabbi Yitzchak lists four things that tear up a person's decree: charity, crying out (*tze'akah*), a change of name, and a change of deeds. Some add a change of place. The proof texts are Proverbs 10:2, Psalms 107:28, Genesis 17:15 (Sarah) and Jonah 3:10. [Rosh Hashanah 16b]

**Connection to *Unetaneh Tokef*.** The piyyut (liturgical poem) says that repentance, prayer and charity "avert the severity of the decree". This is from the text of the prayer, which I did not retrieve here. I do not claim that the Talmud's list is its direct source, only that they share the idea. The piyyut is traditionally attributed to Rabbi Amnon of Mainz, but the story is a later legend and the authorship is uncertain.

**Insights for the service:**
- The piyyut lists the possible fates (*mi yichyeh u'mi yamut*, "who shall live and who shall die"). It then says the outcome is not fixed, because three actions can change it.
- The three actions are inner, vertical and horizontal. Teshuvah changes who I am, tefillah changes my relationship with God, and tzedakah changes my relationship with others.
- The Talmud's "change of name" can be read as becoming a different person, so that the person judged is not the same one who sinned. This is my gloss, not a quotation from a source.

*Practice note.* *Unetaneh Tokef* is said in Ashkenazi communities and in Chabad. In Sephardi communities practice varies by community, so check your own custom.

## 5. Avinu Malkeinu (from memory, not retrieved here)
*Avinu Malkeinu* is a prayer of repeated appeals to God as both Father and King. It is traditionally linked to Rabbi Akiva's prayer during a drought (Taanit 25b), which I did not retrieve here. It is usually omitted on Shabbat, which is worth mentioning because Rosh Hashanah may fall on Shabbat.

**Insight.** The prayer holds two images together. A King brings justice and awe, and a Father brings closeness, and Rosh Hashanah needs both. "Our Father" comes first, so we approach as children before we approach as subjects.

## Suggested flow for the service (about 10 minutes)
1. Ask the room "Why does judgment begin with coronation?" and teach the three themes (section 1).
2. Teach "judged as you are now" and the three books (section 3).
3. Use the "tear up the decree" teaching as the emotional high point (section 4).
4. Close with the double shofar blowing as an expression of love for the mitzvah (section 2).

If you tell me the length, the audience (age, background) and your nusach, I can turn this into a polished short *dvar Torah* with Hebrew text and translation. For any questions of practice in your community, consult your rabbi.

answer:
**The Amidah** (*Amidah*, "standing") is the central prayer of Jewish worship. It is also called *Shemoneh Esrei* ("Eighteen") and simply *Tefillah* ("the Prayer"). Jews say it standing, facing Jerusalem, and silently. It is a series of blessings that praise God, ask for our needs, and give thanks. It is said at every weekday, Shabbat, and holiday service.

## Key Takeaways
- The Amidah is a fixed sequence of blessings. It was originally 18, and a 19th was added later. Weekdays have 19, and Shabbat and holidays have 7.
- Its structure is three blessings of praise, then petitions, then three blessings of thanks.
- The Rabbis trace its formulation to Ezra and his court, and its times to the Patriarchs or to the Temple offerings.
- It is said three times daily (Shacharit, Minchah, Maariv), with an added *Musaf* on Shabbat, Rosh Chodesh, and holidays.

## Source and purpose
Rambam explains that prayer itself is a Torah commandment, learned from "serve Him with all your heart" (Deuteronomy 11:13). The Torah does not set the number of prayers, the wording, or the times. Originally each person prayed in their own words, praising God, asking for their needs, and then giving thanks. After the Babylonian exile, many Jews could no longer express themselves well in Hebrew. So "Ezra and his court established eighteen blessings in sequence" so that everyone, eloquent or not, could pray a complete prayer ([Mishneh Torah, Prayer and the Priestly Blessing 1:1-4]). In Rambam's words: "The first three are praises of God and the last three are thanksgiving. The intermediate [blessings] contain requests for… the desires of each and every person and the needs of the whole community."

## Structure
- **First three blessings (praise):** Avot (God of the Patriarchs), Gevurot (God's power, including resurrection and rain), and Kedushat HaShem (God's holiness).
- **Middle blessings (petitions) on weekdays:** These ask for wisdom, repentance, forgiveness, redemption, healing, a good year, the ingathering of exiles, justice, the removal of wrongdoers, the righteous, the rebuilding of Jerusalem, the Davidic kingdom, and the acceptance of prayer. The "eighteen" became nineteen when a blessing against slanderers was added. On Shabbat and holidays these are replaced by a single blessing about the day's holiness.
- **Last three blessings (thanks):** Avodah (desire for acceptance of our service), Hoda'ah (thanksgiving), and Birkat Shalom (peace).

Many people then add personal prayers before stepping back.

## The three daily times
The Talmud records two views on the origin of the three prayers ([Berakhot 26b]):
- **Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Chanina:** The Patriarchs instituted them. Abraham set Shacharit, Isaac set Minchah, and Jacob set Maariv, each based on a verse.
- **Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi:** The prayers correspond to the daily Temple offerings, such as the morning *tamid* and the afternoon *tamid*. This is why Musaf matches the additional offerings.

The Talmud suggests the two views can be reconciled: the Patriarchs established the prayers, and the Rabbis linked them to the offerings.

## Practice
Customs vary by community. Ashkenaz, Sefard, and Edot HaMizrach have somewhat different wording. Some communities repeat the Amidah aloud, and some add other insertions. Many siddurim have a clear English translation, and a beginner can start with the first blessing and build from there. For your own practice, consult your rabbi.

answer:
You most likely mean **Modeh Ani** (מודה אני), the short thank-you prayer said on waking. Judaism has other thanksgiving prayers too, listed below. I'm assuming Modeh Ani, so tell me if you meant a different one.

## Key Takeaways
- Modeh Ani is a one-sentence thanks to God for returning your soul each morning.
- It is said right on waking, before washing and before any other prayer.
- The word *modeh* means both "I thank" and "I admit or acknowledge."
- Other thank-you prayers include *Modim* in the Amidah, *Birkat HaGomel*, and *Birkat Hamazon*.

## The text (Modeh Ani)
The Sefaria Siddur Ashkenaz has a longer form. The common short version is:

> מוֹדֶה אֲנִי לְפָנֶיךָ מֶלֶךְ חַי וְקַיָּם שֶׁהֶחֱזַרְתָּ בִּי נִשְׁמָתִי בְּחֶמְלָה, רַבָּה אֱמוּנָתֶךָ
> "I give thanks before You, living and everlasting King, for You have restored my soul within me with mercy. Great is Your faithfulness."

The version in [Siddur Ashkenaz, Weekday, Shacharit, Preparatory Prayers, Modeh Ani] adds "The beginning of wisdom is fear of Adonoy…" and "Blessed be the Name of His glorious kingdom…". Women say *modah* instead of *modeh*.

## Meaning
- **Sleep and the soul:** The prayer reflects a traditional idea that sleep is a small taste of death. Waking up means God has returned your soul to you. This is a customary understanding, not something I verified in a specific source here.
- **Faith:** "Great is Your faithfulness" means God trusts you with another day, and you trust Him to give it.
- **Why it is said right away:** It has no Divine Name, so it can be said before handwashing and before you are ritually clean. It is also said in bed, before getting up.

## Other "thank you" prayers
- **Modim** is the thanksgiving blessing in the Amidah. It thanks God for daily miracles.
- **Birkat HaGomel** is said by someone who survived danger. The Talmud says four people must give thanks: those who crossed the sea, travelled the desert, recovered from illness, or were released from prison. The source is Rav Yehudah in [Berakhot 54b].
- **Hodu** is the biblical call to thank God: "Praise God, who is good, whose steadfast love is eternal" [Psalms 136:1]. It opens Hallel and parts of the morning service.
- **Birkat Hamazon** is the thanks after a meal.

If you want, I can go through the Modim prayer or Birkat HaGomel in detail. For questions about how to practice these, consult your rabbi.

answer:
The Kaddish is an Aramaic doxology that praises and "sanctifies" God's great name and prays for His kingdom to be established. It is not a prayer for the dead by origin. It is a core public prayer, recited with a *minyan* (a quorum of ten), and it divides the sections of the prayer service. Over the centuries it became customary for mourners to recite it as well.

## Key Takeaways
- Kaddish is mostly in Aramaic and centers on the congregation's response: "*Yehe shmei rabba mevarach…*" ("May His great name be blessed forever…").
- It is said only with a minyan, because it is a public sanctification of God's name.
- It marks transitions in the service, and there are several forms: Half, Full, Rabbinic, Mourner's and the Burial Kaddish.
- The mourner's Kaddish is a later custom, and it contains no mention of death.
- Nusach (wording and customs) varies by community, so check your own siddur.

## What it says
The opening, as quoted by Rambam, is:

> יִתְגַדַּל וְיִתְקַדַּשׁ שְׁמֵיהּ רַבָּא בְּעָלְמָא דִּבְרָא כִרְעוּתֵיהּ וְיַמְלִיךְ מַלְכוּתֵיהּ וְיַצְמַח פּוּרְקָנֵיהּ וִיקָרֵב מְשִׁיחֵיהּ… בַּעֲגָלָא וּבִזְמַן קָרִיב וְאִמְרוּ אָמֵן
> [Mishneh Torah, The Order of Prayer 2:33]

My translation: "May His great name be magnified and sanctified in the world that He created according to His will. May He establish His kingdom, cause His redemption to sprout, and bring near His anointed one… speedily and soon, and say: Amen."

The congregation then answers: "*Yehe shmei rabba mevarach le'alam ule'almei almaya*" ("May His great name be blessed forever and to all eternity"). The leader continues with a series of praise words (blessed, praised, glorified, exalted…) and a closing request for peace: "*Oseh shalom bimromav…*".

The language echoes Ezekiel's vision of God's name being magnified and sanctified, in [Ezekiel 38:23].

## Why it matters: the congregational response
The Talmud treats the response "*Yehe shmei rabba*" as extremely precious. In [Berakhot 3a], Elijah tells Rabbi Yose that when Israel enters synagogues and study halls and answers "*yehe shmei hagadol mevorach*," God shakes His head and says that happy is the king who is praised this way in his house. The passage sits in a context of God's sorrow over the Temple's destruction.

The halachic literature says to answer with full concentration. The Beit Yosef quotes Rabbeinu Yonah that "with all his strength" means with all one's intention, not necessarily loudly [Beit Yosef, Orach Chayim 56:3:1]. The Mishnah Berurah adds that the custom is to answer "Amen" after "*yitbarach*" and also after the opening *yitgadal*, and notes that the Shulchan Arukh omitted this [Mishnah Berurah 56:12].

## Forms and uses
- **Half Kaddish** marks a break within the service, for example before the Amidah or after the Torah reading.
- **Full Kaddish** ends a section of prayer and adds a request that our prayers be accepted.
- **Rabbinic Kaddish** is said after studying Torah or Talmud, and it adds a prayer for teachers and students.
- **Mourner's Kaddish** is said by mourners, traditionally for 11 months after a parent's death and on the *yahrzeit* (the anniversary of the death). The custom arose in medieval Ashkenaz, where it came to be understood as honoring the deceased by leading the congregation in sanctifying God's name. I did not verify the sources for this history in this session. The prayer is about God's greatness, and mourners affirm it even in grief.
- **Burial Kaddish** is a longer version said at a funeral and at a completed Talmud study. Its wording differs from the others.

## Practical notes
- It requires a minyan. In many communities, women and non-mourners also respond with "Amen" and "*Yehe shmei rabba*."
- Nusach and customs (who says Mourner's Kaddish, and whether mourners say it together) vary between communities, so follow your local practice.

For your personal situation, such as saying Kaddish for a relative, consult your rabbi.

answer:
Le nom יְהוָה ne se lit pas tel qu'il est écrit. La voyelle que vous cherchez est le *holam* (le point au-dessus), qui donne יְהֹוָה, mais cette voyelle n'indique pas une prononciation. Dans la lecture et la prière, on lit « *Adonaï* » (אֲדֹנָי). Dans la conversation, on dit « *HaShem* » (« le Nom »).

## Points essentiels

- La voyelle « manquante » est le *holam* (ֹ) sur le ה. C'est celui du mot אֲדֹנָי.
- Les voyelles du Tétragramme dans le texte massorétique sont empruntées à *Adonaï*. Elles rappellent au lecteur quel mot dire à la place du Nom. Elles ne transcrivent pas sa prononciation d'origine.
- Le Talmud dit explicitement que le Nom n'est pas lu comme il est écrit.
- La prononciation d'origine n'est pas transmise publiquement. « Yehovah » ou « Jéhovah » est une forme hybride, non une lecture traditionnelle.

## Explication

**1. La voyelle manquante.** Votre graphie יְהוָה porte un *chewa* sous le י et un *kamats* sous le ה final. Le *holam* est absent. Beaucoup d'éditions le notent sur le premier ה : יְהֹוָה. Ce sont les voyelles d'אֲדֹנָי : le *hataf-patah* devient un simple *chewa* sous le י, puis viennent le *holam* et le *kamats*. L'explication est de moi, pas d'une source citée ici. Cette vocalisation est un signal de lecture (*qeré*) : « lis *Adonaï* ». Quand le texte porte déjà אֲדֹנָי juste avant, on le vocalise avec les voyelles d'*Elohim* (יֱהֹוִה), pour éviter de dire deux fois « Adonaï ».

**2. Ce que dit le Talmud.** Dans [Kiddushin 71a], Rabbi Yohanan dit que les Sages ne transmettent le nom de quatre lettres à leurs élèves qu'une fois par semaine, ou deux selon une autre opinion. Le Talmud cite ensuite le verset « זֶה שְׁמִי לְעֹלָם », en notant que « לְעַלֵּם » est écrit, ce qui suggère « à cacher ». Il ajoute cette parole que le Saint béni soit-Il prononce :

« לֹא כְּשֶׁאֲנִי נִכְתָּב אֲנִי נִקְרָא, נִכְתָּב אֲנִי בְּיוֹד הֵי וְנִקְרָא בְּאָלֶף דָּלֶת »

(Traduction littérale de ma part : « Je ne suis pas lu comme je suis écrit. Je suis écrit avec *yod-hé* et lu avec *alef-dalet*. »)

Le Talmud précise aussi que du temps du Temple, ce nom était dit par les prêtres, et que les plus discrets d'entre eux le noyaient dans la mélodie de leurs frères. Après la destruction du Temple, cet usage a cessé. Je cite aussi de mémoire que la Mishna ([Mishnah Sanhedrin 10:1]) range celui qui prononce le Nom comme il s'écrit parmi ceux qui n'ont pas de part au monde à venir. Je n'ai pas pu retrouver ce texte à l'instant, donc vérifiez-le.

**3. Comment le dire en pratique.**
- Pour la lecture de la Torah, la prière et les bénédictions, on dit « *Adonaï* ».
- Pour une conversation, un cours ou une citation, on dit « *HaShem* ».
- On ne cherche pas à reconstituer le Nom. Cette prononciation ne s'apprend pas à partir de la vocalisation écrite.

Pour votre situation personnelle, consultez votre rabbin.

answer:
**Réponse directe :** la séquence « Alef‑Hé‑Vav‑Yod » (אהוי) n'est pas un Nom divin connu de la tradition. Je n'ai trouvé aucune source qui l'atteste. Il s'agit sans doute d'une confusion avec l'un de ces deux Noms :
- *Ehyeh* (אהיה : Alef‑Hé‑Yod‑Hé), le Nom de [Exodus 3:14] ;
- le Tétragramme (יהוה : Yod‑Hé‑Vav‑Hé), dont les lettres Hé, Vav et Yod figurent dans votre séquence.

## Points clés
- Le Nom *Ehyeh* s'écrit Alef‑Hé‑Yod‑Hé et signifie « Je serai ».
- Le Tétragramme s'écrit Yod‑Hé‑Vav‑Hé. C'est le Nom de l'Être, et on ne le prononce pas tel qu'il est écrit.
- Si vous avez vu « אהוי » quelque part, il faut vérifier le contexte : faute de copie, abréviation ou autre. Ne le traitez pas comme un Nom sacré établi.

## Le Nom *Ehyeh* (le plus proche de votre demande)
Au buisson ardent, Moïse demande comment nommer D.ieu au peuple. La réponse est :

« וַיֹּאמֶר אֱלֹהִים אֶל־מֹשֶׁה אֶהְיֶה אֲשֶׁר אֶהְיֶה, וַיֹּאמֶר כֹּה תֹאמַר לִבְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל אֶהְיֶה שְׁלָחַנִי אֲלֵיכֶם »
(traduction) « D.ieu dit à Moïse : *Ehyeh‑Asher‑Ehyeh* ; et Il dit : Ainsi tu diras aux enfants d'Israël : *Ehyeh* m'a envoyé vers vous. » [Exodus 3:14]

- **Racine :** ה‑י‑ה (*hayah*), « être ». *Ehyeh* est la première personne du futur : « Je serai ». D.ieu se présente comme Celui qui sera présent avec Israël, y compris dans l'exil à venir. C'est l'explication que je connais chez Rashi, mais je n'ai pas pu relire son commentaire ici, donc je ne le cite pas mot à mot.
- **Dans la Kabbale :** *Ehyeh* est associé à la séfira de *Keter* (la « Couronne »), la plus haute, comme source de ce qui n'existe pas encore. C'est la lecture kabbalistique courante. Je ne cite pas ici de passage précis.

## Le Tétragramme (Yod‑Hé‑Vav‑Hé)
Ses lettres sont celles du verbe « être » aux trois temps : *hayah* (il fut), *hoveh* (il est), *yihyeh* (il sera). C'est pourquoi on y voit le Nom de l'Éternité. Dans la pratique, on le lit « *Adonaï* », et hors de la prière, on dit « *Hachem* » (« le Nom »).

## Pour aller plus loin
Pouvez‑vous me dire où vous avez rencontré cette séquence (livre, chant, amulette, site) ? Je pourrai alors identifier la source ou l'erreur probable. Je vous déconseille d'utiliser des Noms divins dans des pratiques personnelles, et d'étudier ces sujets avec un maître.

answer:
Oui, c'est une belle observation. Si on retire le *lamed* (ל) de אִילָן (*ilan*, « arbre »), il reste אַיִן (*ayin*, « rien, néant »), c'est-à-dire les lettres א-י-ן. C'est un jeu de lettres (*drash*), pas une preuve. Mais il rejoint des idées connues de la pensée juive.

## Points clés
- Le mot *ilan* contient les lettres de *ayin* (א-י-ן), plus un *lamed*.
- En Kabbale et en hassidut, *Ayin* désigne le « néant » divin, source de toute existence, d'où l'expression *yesh me'ayin* (« l'être à partir du néant »).
- Cela cadre bien avec l'image de l'arbre : l'arbre qui part d'une graine « disparue » est une image classique de la création.

## Développement

**Le calcul.** א (1) + י (10) + ל (30) + ן (50) = 91. Sans le ל, on a 1 + 10 + 50 = 61, la valeur de *ayin*. Le ל, qui vaut 30, est la lettre la plus haute de l'alphabet hébreu. On peut donc lire que l'« arbre » est un « néant » auquel s'ajoute une « élévation » : l'être déployé à partir du rien.

**Autres liens, eux aussi homilétiques.** 91 est la valeur de *amen* (אמן : 1 + 40 + 50). C'est aussi la somme des valeurs des Noms divins YHVH (26) et Adonaï (65). Ces rapprochements sont courants dans la tradition, mais ils relèvent de l'homélie.

**Le sens littéral.** *Ilan* est un mot de la langue de la Mishna et du Talmud, d'origine araméenne. La Torah emploie plutôt *etz* (עץ) pour « arbre ». La proximité avec *ayin* n'a donc rien d'étymologique.

**L'image de l'arbre en Kabbale.** Les sefirot sont souvent représentées comme un « arbre » (*ilan haSefirot*). Leur sommet, *Keter*, est associé à l'*Ayin*, ce qui rend ton rapprochement d'autant plus parlant.

Si tu veux, je peux chercher des sources précises sur *Ayin* et *yesh me'ayin* dans la littérature hassidique.

answer:
Dans [Exodus 3:15], « זֶה־שְּׁמִי לְעֹלָם וְזֶה זִכְרִי לְדֹר דֹּר » est la réponse finale de Dieu à la question de Moïse : « Quel est Son nom ? ». Le verset désigne le Nom de quatre lettres, יהוה (le Tétragramme). Pour le *pshat* (sens simple), ce Nom, lié aux patriarches, restera l'identité de Dieu pour Israël à jamais. Pour la tradition talmudique, le mot « לְעֹלָם » est écrit sans *vav* (« לעלם »), ce qui suggère « cacher » (*le'alem*) : on ne prononce pas ce Nom comme il est écrit.

## Points clés
- Le verset vient après deux réponses : « אֶהְיֶה אֲשֶׁר אֶהְיֶה » (v. 14), puis le Nom יהוה uni au « Dieu de vos pères » (v. 15).
- Pour le *pshat* de Rashbam, Ramban et Sforno, le verset parle de la mémoire éternelle du lien entre Dieu et les patriarches.
- Selon le Talmud et Rashi, l'écriture défective de « לעלם » enseigne de cacher le Nom, lu « Adonaï ».
- Le Hamek Davar lit les deux moitiés du verset comme deux modes de conduite divine.

## Le contexte
Moïse demande : « וְאָמְרוּ־לִי מַה־שְּׁמוֹ מָה אֹמַר אֲלֵהֶם » (« S'ils me demandent : quel est Son nom ? que leur dirai-je ? »). Dieu répond d'abord « אֶהְיֶה אֲשֶׁר אֶהְיֶה » et « אֶהְיֶה שְׁלָחַנִי אֲלֵיכֶם ». Puis Il dit « עוֹד » (« encore ») : « יְהֹוָה אֱלֹהֵי אֲבֹתֵיכֶם… שְׁלָחַנִי אֲלֵיכֶם, זֶה־שְּׁמִי לְעֹלָם וְזֶה זִכְרִי לְדֹר דֹּר » [Exodus 3:13-15]. Traduction du texte : « Voici Mon nom pour toujours, voici Mon appellation de génération en génération. »

Les deux termes sont en parallèle : « שֵׁם » (nom) et « זֵכֶר » (mémoire, mention). Rashi note que « זכרי » peut signifier « la mention de Moi » : le nom est ce par quoi on invoque et on se souvient de Dieu [Rashi on Exodus 3:15:2]. Il rapproche le verset du Psaume 135:13 : « יְהוָה שִׁמְךָ לְעוֹלָם, יְהוָה זִכְרְךָ לְדֹר וָדֹר ».

## Lecture talmudique : « לעלם » = cacher
Le mot « לְעֹלָם » est écrit ici sans *vav* (לעלם). Rashi explique que cela suggère « לְעַלֵּם » : « Ceci est Mon nom *qui doit être caché* ». On ne doit donc pas le lire comme il est écrit, mais comme « Adonaï ». Selon Rashi, « וזה זכרי » enseigne à Moïse comment le Nom doit être lu [Rashi on Exodus 3:15:1-2].

Le Talmud contient cet enseignement. Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak dit : « Ce monde-ci n'est pas comme le monde à venir. Dans ce monde, [le Nom] s'écrit avec *yod-hé* et se lit avec *alef-dalet*. Dans le monde à venir, tout sera un : il se lira *yod-hé* et s'écrira *yod-hé* » [Pesachim 50a]. Il commente ainsi « וּשְׁמוֹ אֶחָד » de Zacharie 14:9. Le même passage rapporte que Rava voulait expliquer publiquement le Nom, et qu'un vieillard lui répondit : « "לְעַלֵּם" כְּתִיב » (« c'est écrit : *à cacher* »). La suite du texte, tronquée dans ma consultation, cite aussi le rapprochement entre « זה שמי לעלם » et « וזה זכרי ». Je ne la cite donc pas ici.

Dans un registre homilétique, le Kitzur Ba'al HaTurim remarque que la valeur numérique de « זה » (7 + 5 = 12) évoque un Nom de douze lettres transmis à Moïse [Kitzur Ba'al HaTurim on Exodus 3:15:1]. C'est une allusion (*drash*), pas une preuve.

## Lecture du *pshat* chez les commentateurs
- **Rashbam** distingue les deux réponses. « אהיה אשר אהיה » exprime l'essence de Dieu. Le nom du verset 15, יהוה, exprime Sa royauté, par laquelle on Le mentionne (comme on mentionne un roi par son titre) [Rashbam on Exodus 3:15:2-3].
- **Ibn Ezra** y voit un passage fondamental sur la nature d'un nom propre. Les noms « אהיה » et « יהוה » ont selon lui la même racine de sens (l'être). L'un est à la première personne, l'autre à la troisième. Il explique aussi que Dieu seul existe éternellement et que l'existence de tout dépend de Lui [Ibn Ezra on Exodus 3:15:1-3].
- **Ramban** fait de « וזה זכרי » un renvoi à « Dieu d'Abraham, d'Isaac et de Jacob ». L'alliance avec les patriarches ne sera jamais oubliée : chaque génération d'Israël les mentionnera dans la prière [Ramban on Exodus 3:15:1].
- **Sforno** ajoute que ce nom s'ajoute aux attributs déjà mentionnés. L'alliance avec les patriarches et leurs descendants fait partie de la définition de Dieu, « à jamais » [Sforno on Exodus 3:15:2].
- **Hamek Davar** insiste sur la coupure du verset. Il ne dit pas « זה שמי וזכרי לדור דור », il le divise en deux. Selon lui, יהוה, Dieu de vos pères, désigne une conduite dans la nature avec providence individuelle, et celle-ci est « לעולם ». Les modes « Dieu d'Abraham, d'Isaac, de Jacob » relèvent de voies plus élevées, miraculeuses et plus rares [Haamek Davar on Exodus 3:15:6].

## En pratique
La tradition en tire l'usage de ne pas prononcer le Nom comme il est écrit. Dans la prière et la lecture de la Torah, on dit « Adonaï ». Hors de ces contextes, beaucoup disent « HaShem » (« le Nom »). Pour les détails pratiques, consulte ton rabbin.

**The standard spelling is only with an aleph: אין סוף (*Ein Sof*), meaning "without end."** A spelling with ayin, עין סוף, would not mean "endless." It would read "eye of the end," which is a different phrase. The two spellings are not interchangeable, though the Hebrew wordplay between them is real.

## Key Takeaways
- *Ein* (אין, aleph-yud-nun) means "there is not" or "without." This is the word in *Ein Sof* and *Ohr Ein Sof* (אור אין סוף), "the light of the Infinite."
- *Ayin* (עין, ayin-yud-nun) means "eye" or "spring." It is a different word, and it does not carry the sense of "without."
- The two words sound alike and share the letters yud and nun, so kabbalistic and chassidic writers sometimes play on them.
- The same aleph/ayin pair appears in אור (*or*, light) and עור (*or*, skin). In Genesis 3:21 the word is usually read as עור, "skins of," but a midrashic tradition about Rabbi Meir's Torah scroll reads it as אור, "light." I'm citing that from memory and haven't checked it here.

## Details

**Why it's an aleph.** *Ohr* (אור) is "light" and *Ein Sof* (אין סוף) is "without end." Together they give "the light that has no end." Kabbalah uses *Ein Sof* as a name for God as He is before and beyond any limitation, and *Ohr Ein Sof* for the divine light that emanates from Him. The word *ein* is the same one used for "nothing" or "there is not." Nothing in the phrase calls for an ayin.

**Where the confusion may come from.** In pronunciation, many Hebrew speakers and transliterations render both aleph and ayin as a soft "a." In English, "Ain Sof" and "Ayin" can look alike. The letters also relate in the kabbalistic idea of *Ayin* (אין, "nothingness") as the highest, hidden level of divinity. That spelling still uses an aleph, and it is a separate concept from *Ein Sof*.

**If you saw עין סוף somewhere.** It may be a typo, or a deliberate pun. If you tell me where you saw it, I can look at the source with you. I don't know of a classical source that treats עין סוף as a legitimate variant of אין סוף. If you have one in mind, I'd be glad to look at it.

The two words sound a little alike, but they aren't related in Hebrew. *Yissurim* (יִסּוּרִים, suffering or chastisement) comes from the root י-ס-ר. *Yerushalayim* (יְרוּשָׁלַיִם, Jerusalem) has a different root. There is a real thematic link between suffering and the Land of Israel, but it is a teaching of the Rabbis, not a matter of etymology.

## Key Takeaways
- *Yissurim* comes from י-ס-ר, meaning to discipline, correct, or chastise.
- *Yerushalayim* is usually explained as a combination of two names, not from י-ס-ר.
- The overlap is the letters י and ר and the sound, which is coincidence.
- The Talmud does link suffering with acquiring the Land of Israel, which may be what you have in mind.

## The word *yissurim*
The root י-ס-ר gives *musar* (מוּסָר, instruction or discipline) and *yissur* (יִסּוּר, chastisement). The verb is used for a parent's correction, as in Proverbs 3:11, "מוּסַר ה' בְּנִי אַל תִּמְאָס". The sense is "discipline that teaches," and that is why Jewish tradition speaks of *yissurin shel ahavah* (suffering of love). In later Hebrew the word came to mean suffering in general.

## The name *Yerushalayim*
The traditional explanations are:
- **A combination of two names.** One view joins *Yireh*, the name Avraham gave the mountain (Genesis 22:14), with *Shalem*, the city of Malki-Tzedek (Genesis 14:18). I am recalling this from the midrashic tradition and did not look it up in this chat, so check it before relying on it.
- **Shalem and shalom.** The name is often linked to *shalem* (whole) and *shalom* (peace).

Neither explanation involves י-ס-ר. Hebrew words with similar letters often have unrelated roots.

## Where suffering and the Land do connect
The Talmud teaches that three good gifts were given to Israel only through suffering: Torah, the Land of Israel, and the World to Come. I believe this is in Berakhot 5a, but my lookup of the page failed, so I haven't checked the wording. This is a homiletic link between *yissurim* and the Land. It does not make the words related.

If you had a different Hebrew word in mind, such as *Moriah*, *Yisrael*, or *Yeshurun*, tell me and I'll look at that one.

**"Sead" most likely means the Hebrew *se'ad* (סְעָד), "to support, sustain, or refresh," especially with food.** It is the root of *se'udah* (סְעוּדָה), a "meal." You may have meant something else, so tell me if you did. I could only retrieve one source before the lookup tool was rate-limited.

## Key Takeaways
- The root סעד means to support or sustain.
- In the Torah it refers to strengthening oneself with food.
- *Se'udah* (a meal) comes from this root.
- In Hebrew today, *sa'ad* can also mean to give social or welfare support.

## The word in the text
The clearest example is Abraham welcoming his guests:

> "וְאֶקְחָה פַת־לֶחֶם וְסַעֲדוּ לִבְּכֶם אַחַר תַּעֲבֹרוּ"
> "Let me fetch a morsel of bread that you may refresh yourselves; then go on." [Genesis 18:5]

Here *sa'adu libchem* (סַעֲדוּ לִבְּכֶם) literally means "support your heart." The heart stands for a person's vitality, and bread is what holds it up. The same sense appears in the Bible's other uses of the root. Psalms 18:36 has *yimnekha yisadeni* ("Your right hand supports me"). I couldn't retrieve that verse to quote it, so check it yourself.

## Related words
- ***Se'udah*** (סְעוּדָה): a meal, as in *se'udat mitzvah*, *se'udah shlishit*, and *se'udat Purim*. The name comes from the idea of sustaining the body.
- ***Sa'ad / sa'ad*** (סַעַד): support or aid. In modern Hebrew, *sa'ad* is also used for welfare and social services.

**Deker** (דֶּקֶר) comes from the root ד־ק־ר, which means "to pierce" or "to stab." As a name, it appears in the Tanakh only as the father of one of Solomon's officials, "Ben-Deker" (literally "son of Deker"). It isn't a common given name, and I know of no classical tradition that gives it a special significance.

## Key Takeaways
- The root ד־ק־ר means to pierce or thrust through.
- The only biblical appearance of the name is in "Ben-Deker," an administrator under King Solomon.
- The name carries no known classical drash (homiletical interpretation), so any "significance" is limited to its linguistic meaning.
- In modern Hebrew, *dakar* (דקר) still means "to stab," and *maddeker* or *dekar* can refer to a stabbing tool.

## Meaning and root
The verb appears in the Torah when Pinchas kills Zimri and Cozbi: "וַיִּדְקֹר אֶת־שְׁנֵיהֶם" ("and he pierced the two of them") [Numbers 25:8]. Lamentations uses it for being pierced by arrows: "דקר אותי בחיצים" [Lamentations 3:13]. It also appears in the passive form *meduqarim* ("pierced") in [Lamentations 4:9]. These are biblical Hebrew uses. The core idea is a sharp, penetrating thrust, so *Deker* literally means something like "a piercing" or "a stabbing."

## The biblical appearance
"בֶּן־דֶּקֶר בְּמָקַץ וּבְשַׁעַלְבִים וּבֵית שָׁמֶשׁ וְאֵילוֹן בֵּית חָנָן" ("Ben-deker, in Makaz, Shaalbim, Beth-shemesh, and Elon-beth-hanan") [I Kings 4:9]. He is one of the twelve district officers who supplied Solomon's court. The verse gives no further detail about him. Some translators and commentators take "Ben-Deker" as a personal name, and the Hebrew itself is not explicit that it is not a title. I haven't checked the commentators on this verse, so I can't say what any of them say about it.

## Significance
- **Linguistic:** The name belongs to a family of Hebrew names built on concrete nouns from physical actions.
- **Homiletical:** Any spiritual reading, such as zeal like Pinchas's, would be my own association and not a source-based tradition. I wouldn't present it as established.

**Salmo 32 (Tehilim 32)** es un salmo de David sobre la confesión y el perdón. El que calla su pecado sufre, y el que lo reconoce ante Dios recibe perdón y alegría. La traducción que sigue es mía, hecha a partir del hebreo y de la versión inglesa de Sefaria, porque Sefaria no tiene versión en español de este texto. Ver [Psalms 32:1-11].

## Puntos clave
- Es un *maskil* (poema instructivo) de David sobre la teshuvá (arrepentimiento).
- El silencio ante el pecado destruye por dentro; la confesión trae perdón.
- Dios es refugio y guía para quien confiesa.
- No hay que ser como el caballo o la mula que necesitan freno para acercarse.
- Termina con alegría para los justos y los rectos de corazón.

## Traducción

1. De David. *Maskil*. Feliz aquel cuya transgresión es perdonada, cuyo pecado es cubierto.
2. Feliz la persona a quien el Eterno no le cuenta culpa, y en cuyo espíritu no hay engaño.
3. Mientras callé, mis huesos se consumieron por mi rugido todo el día.
4. Porque de día y de noche tu mano pesaba sobre mí; mi vigor se transformó como en la sequía del verano. *Sela*.
5. Mi pecado te hice saber y no encubrí mi culpa. Dije: «Confesaré mis transgresiones al Eterno», y Tú perdonaste la culpa de mi pecado. *Sela*.
6. Por eso todo fiel rezará a Ti en el momento oportuno [lit. «de hallar»]; entonces, aunque desborden las muchas aguas, a él no llegarán.
7. Tú eres refugio para mí; de la angustia me guardas; con cantos de liberación me rodeas. *Sela*.
8. Te haré entender y te enseñaré el camino por el que andarás; te aconsejaré, con mi ojo puesto sobre ti.
9. No seáis como caballo o mula sin entendimiento, cuyo ímpetu se sujeta con freno y brida, para que no se acerquen a ti.
10. Muchos son los dolores del malvado, pero al que confía en el Eterno, la bondad lo rodeará.
11. Alegraos en el Eterno y regocijaos, justos; cantad con júbilo, todos los rectos de corazón.

## Comentario breve
- **Estructura:** los versículos 1-2 son una declaración de dicha. Los versículos 3-5 cuentan la experiencia personal: callar causa sufrimiento y confesar trae perdón. Los versículos 6-7 y 8-9 son enseñanza y consejo. Los versículos 10-11 cierran con una conclusión.
- **El versículo 5** resume el proceso de teshuvá: reconocer el pecado, no encubrirlo y confesarlo. Por eso este salmo se cita con frecuencia en el contexto del arrepentimiento.
- **El versículo 9** compara a quien necesita ser forzado con el caballo y la mula. Dios pide un acercamiento libre y consciente.
- **Palabras difíciles:** *«le-et metzó»* (v. 6) se interpreta de varias maneras. Puede referirse al momento de hallar el pecado o al momento en que Dios se deja hallar. No he consultado aquí a los comentaristas (Rashi, Ibn Ezra, Radak), así que no les atribuyo ninguna interpretación concreta.

Si quieres, puedo buscar lo que dicen Rashi, Radak o Ibn Ezra sobre este salmo.

answer:
This is my own translation of the full text, which I retrieved from Sefaria [Kitzur Baal HaTurim on Deuteronomy 5:16]. The passage ties the honor of parents to the child's own origins. A child should honor parents who took care to avoid nine improper marital states, and the child owes them honor in nine ways.

## Key Takeaways
- "Honor your father" is placed next to Shabbat because honor includes food and clothing.
- The extra *tet* in "*yitav*" (it will be good) hints at the nine months of pregnancy and at nine marital conduct-flaws.
- The nine flaws have the mnemonic *Asnat Mishgach*, and the passage explains each one.
- The extra words in the second version of the Ten Commandments total 17, the numerical value of *tov* (good).
- The ending links the verse to "You shall not murder," which follows it.

## Translation

**"סמך כבד את אביך לשבת…"**
It placed "Honor your father" next to Shabbat, because in connection with Shabbat too it is written "*vekhibadto*" (and you shall honor it). This teaches that one must honor him with food and clothing.

**"ולמען ייטב לך"**
The *tet* in "*yitav*" is dotted [lit. "crowned"] because his mother carried him nine months. His father and mother also guarded themselves from the nine traits mentioned in *Nedarim*. Their mnemonic is **אסנ"ת משגע"ח**, an acronym for:

1. children of a coerced woman (*anusa*)
2. children of a hated woman (*senu'a*)
3. children of a *niddah*
4. children of substitution (*temura*)
5. children of quarreling (*merivah*)
6. children of drunkenness (*shikhrut*)
7. children of a woman the husband intends to divorce (*gerushat halev*)
8. children of confusion (*irbuvya*)
9. children of a brazen woman (*chatzufa*)

**Explanation of each:**

1. **Children of a coerced woman.** This is not only about a man who rapes a woman and fathers a son by her. It applies even if she is his wife and he forced her to relations. So we learned in tractate *Kallah*: "Why do people have children with blemishes? Because he demands her and his wife does not respond to him." [Here "does not respond" means she does not consent to him.] Rabbi Yehudah says: because she says to him during relations, "I am coerced," and so outwardly she is willing but inwardly she is unwilling. Similarly it says in *Eruvin*: "Whoever forces his wife to do a mitzvah act is called a sinner, as it says, 'Also, without knowledge the soul is not good'" [Proverbs 19:2]. So coercion is forbidden even with one's wife. If he needs that act, he should appease her and afterward have relations.
2. **Children of a hated woman.** This is as it sounds: she is hated at the time of relations. But if she is desired at the time of relations, it is permitted even though she is hated [at other times].
3. **Children of a *niddah*.** Such a child is not a *mamzer* by Torah law. Some explain it to mean that one of them is under a ban (*nidui*), since those under a ban are forbidden marital relations. The same applies if one of them is in mourning.
4. **Children of substitution.** He intended [relations with] a forbidden woman, and his wife happened to come to him. Some explain: even if both were his wives, he intended one and the other came to him.
5. **Children of a rebellious woman** (*moredet*, in this version of the text). She said to him, "I do not want you," and yet he has relations with her, so she is with him like a harlot. This holds even if it was with her consent. According to another version, the heading is **children of quarreling**. They quarrel together every time, so this act is like fornication, since it does not come from love.
6. **Children of drunkenness.** Either he or she is drunk.
7. **Children of a woman he plans to divorce.** He has it in his heart to divorce her, even without hatred. An example is one of those who are compelled to divorce, and he resolved to divorce her and then came to her.
8. **Children of confusion.** He has relations with his wife while thinking of another woman, even if both are his wives.
9. **Children of a brazen woman.** She demands him with her mouth, so she is like a harlot, and it is forbidden to keep her. But if a wife appeases him with pleasing words and adorns herself before him so that he will turn his attention to her, our Sages said such a woman bears wise and understanding children, like Leah, from whom Issachar came.

All these nine traits apply even when the couple does not need to fulfill procreation, for example when she is already pregnant. Even so, in all these traits he damages the child, and the child is called a "sinner/offender" (*poshea*).

**Honoring parents in nine ways.** One must also honor them in nine ways: feeding, clothing, and so on, as stated in the first chapter of *Kiddushin*.

**Extra words.** There are 17 extra words in the last version of the Ten Commandments compared with the first. That equals the numerical value of *tov* (good), which is why the verse says here "*lema'an yitav lakh*" (that it may go well with you). That phrase is not in the first version.

**"כאשר צוך ה' אלהיך"**
The final letters (*sofei teivot*) of these words have the numerical value of *marah* (bitter), which is 245.

**"על האדמה וגו'"**
Right after it comes "You shall not murder," because it is written, "and for the land no atonement can be made for the blood [shed on it]" [Numbers 35:33].

## Notes
- **Sources named in the text.** It cites tractate *Kallah*, *Eruvin*, *Nedarim* and *Kiddushin* chapter 1. I did not look these up in the original passages, so I can't confirm how closely the wording matches.
- **The nine flaws.** The list of nine is the Talmud's (see *Nedarim* 20a–b). I did not check it here.
- **Version.** The text above is the abridged *Kitzur* of the Baal HaTurim, not the full commentary.
- **A note on the translation.** Bracketed words are my additions. In item 3, "is dotted" translates "*tagin*", literally "crowns" or "decorative strokes". The Hebrew means the *tet* of *yitav* is marked as special.

- The number matches the "330 million gods" often attributed to Hinduism. Classical Jewish sources do not say this.
- The idea also conflicts with Jewish teaching. God is described as one and without form or body. The verse is "שְׁמַע יִשְׂרָאֵל ה׳ אֱלֹקֵינוּ ה׳ אֶחָד" [Deuteronomy 6:4], and Maimonides says God has no body or form [Mishneh Torah, Foundations of the Torah 1:7-8].

**What the Talmud does say that sounds similar:**
- God appeared at the Sea as a warrior and at Sinai as an elder. The Mekhilta explains this as "I am the same God" in both cases [Mekhilta d'Rabbi Yishmael 20:2]. The Talmud makes a related point about the Sinai revelation, that "the voice went out to each person according to their strength" [Shemot Rabbah 5:9]. These speak of different appearances to people, not of many forms of God.
- Mystical sources speak of many names and *sefirot* (emanations or attributes), but they insist these reveal a single God.

This is my own translation of the full Hebrew text of [Ramban on Genesis 9:5]. Sefaria's English version (Artscroll/Ramban, Chavel) is a good guide for the first part, but the text I received was cut off, so I translated the whole passage from the Hebrew. Explanatory additions are in [square brackets].

**Verse:** "אַךְ אֶת־דִּמְכֶם לְנַפְשֹׁתֵיכֶם אֶדְרֹשׁ…" ("But for your own life-blood I will require a reckoning…") [Genesis 9:5].

---

**1. The word *lenafshoteichem***

"דִּמְכֶם לְנַפְשֹׁתֵיכֶם": "Your blood *lenafshoteichem*" means "your blood, *nafshoteichem*", that is, "your blood, which is your lives." [The *lamed* is superfluous], like "לְכֹל כְּלֵי הַמִּשְׁכָּן" ("for all the vessels of the Tabernacle," [Exodus 27:19]) and "הַשְּׁלִישִׁי לְאַבְשָׁלוֹם" ("the third, Avshalom," [I Chronicles 3:2]).

Alternatively, "*lenafshoteichem*" may mean "*benafshoteichem*", "in your lives." This is because "the life of all flesh is its blood, in its life" [Leviticus 17:14]. Compare "וְכָל דָּם לֹא תֹאכְלוּ בְּכֹל מוֹשְׁבֹתֵיכֶם לָעוֹף וְלַבְּהֵמָה" [Leviticus 7:26], which means "in fowl or in animal."

The correct reading is this: "The blood that is the life within you, I will require." Scripture declares that the blood is the life. It hints that one is liable to death for spilling the blood on which life depends. One is not liable for the blood of limbs on which the soul does not depend.

Our Rabbis ([Bava Kamma 91b]) expounded the verse as referring to one who kills himself: "Your blood, from your own lives, I will require."

**2. "מִיַּד כָּל חַיָּה אֶדְרְשֶׁנּוּ", "From the hand of every beast I will require it"**

I wonder whether the "requiring" is meant literally, "from the hand of the beast" just as "from the hand of man," so that there is punishment in the matter. The beast has no intellect with which to be punished or rewarded.

Perhaps this applies only to the blood of man. Any beast that tears him apart will itself be torn apart, because this is a royal decree. That is the reason for "the ox shall surely be stoned, and its flesh shall not be eaten" [Exodus 21:28]. It is not a monetary penalty against its owner, since even a wild ox is liable to death ([Bava Kamma 44b]). He commanded this to the children of Noah just as to Israel.

On this reading, "שׁוֹפֵךְ דַּם הָאָדָם" ("whoever sheds man's blood") means any shedder, beast or man. Its blood is required by the court and by the hands of Heaven.

**3. A second reading of "from the hand of every beast"**

It is possible that "from the hand of every beast" means the vengeance on the shedder of blood will come at the hand of every beast. Compare "כִּי לָקְחָה מִיַּד ה' כִּפְלַיִם בְּכָל חַטֹּאתֶיהָ" ("for she has received from the hand of the Lord double for all her sins," [Isaiah 40:2]). God is saying: "Your blood I will require and avenge by the hand of every beast. I will send against the murderer all the beasts of the earth, and I will send man against him too, and he will not escape them."

Similar usages:
- "מִכָּל צֹרְרַי הָיִיתִי חֶרְפָּה" [Psalms 31:12], meaning "from [the hand of] all my enemies."
- "זֶה חֵלֶק אָדָם רָשָׁע מֵאֱלֹהִים" [Job 20:29], meaning "from the hand of God."

**4. A third reading, "the secret of the matter"**

Perhaps the requiring "from the hand of the beast" means that the beast should not prey on man, because He set this in their nature.

The secret of the matter is as follows. At creation God gave man "every seed-bearing herb and every tree with seed-bearing fruit" for food. He gave the beasts "every green herb" for food, and Scripture says "וַיְהִי כֵן" ("and it was so," [Genesis 1:30]), because this was their nature and custom.

Now God has told man to slaughter animals, and nature (or custom) has been set so that animals prey on one another. It therefore became necessary to command that the other animals not be prey for man's teeth, and that they fear him and not prey on them. [Ramban's wording here is compressed. The sense is that man now eats animals, and so man's own safety from beasts must be secured by decree.]

God said "אַךְ אֶת־דִּמְכֶם לְנַפְשֹׁתֵיכֶם" to hint that He will not require the blood of one animal from another. So they are left free to prey on one another.

**5. Why the prohibition appears here**

This is why the prohibition on shedding blood is mentioned here: because of the permission to slaughter. It had been the practice to shed blood. According to our Rabbis ([Sanhedrin 56b]), Adam had already been warned about this. But because of the permission of slaughter, it was necessary to say: "I have permitted you to shed the blood of every living thing except your own blood. That is forbidden to you, and the animals too were given no nature to shed it."

answer:
**"Torah"** (*Torah*, תּוֹרָה) is most often translated as "teaching" or "instruction." The common translation "law" is too narrow. The word also names the Five Books of Moses (Genesis through Deuteronomy). In a wider sense it means the whole body of Jewish teaching.

## Key Takeaways
- The root of *Torah* is י-ר-ה (*y-r-h*), "to teach, direct, or shoot an arrow straight," so "teaching/instruction" is its core meaning.
- "Law" comes from the Greek *nomos* in the Septuagint. It captures only part of the meaning.
- *Torah* can mean the Five Books (the Written Torah), all of Tanakh, or the entire tradition, including the Oral Torah.
- Traditionally the Torah has 613 commandments, but it also includes narrative, ethics, and history.

## Meaning and root
The word comes from the root י-ר-ה. In its basic sense it means to throw or shoot, as in "he shall surely be shot" (*yarah yiyareh*). It extends to "directing" someone toward the right path, and so to teaching. Related words include *moreh* (מוֹרֶה, teacher) and *horaah* (הוֹרָאָה, instruction or ruling).

The word is used in this teaching sense in Proverbs: "שְׁמַע בְּנִי מוּסַר אָבִיךָ וְאַל תִּטֹּשׁ תּוֹרַת אִמֶּךָ", "Hear, my son, your father's discipline, and do not forsake your mother's teaching" [Proverbs 1:8]. A mother's *torah* is clearly not a legal code but guidance.

## Different uses of the word
- **Narrow sense:** The Written Torah, the Five Books of Moses (also called *Chumash* or the Pentateuch). The Torah scroll contains these five books.
- **Broader sense:** All of Tanakh, or the whole body of Jewish learning. Tradition includes the Oral Torah (Mishnah, Talmud, Midrash) as part of "Torah."
- **Individual teachings:** For example, "this is the *torah* of the burnt offering" [Leviticus 6:2], meaning the instructions for that offering.

## Why "law" is incomplete
Many older English Bibles render *Torah* as "the Law." This follows the Greek Septuagint, which used *nomos*. Most of Genesis and much of Exodus is narrative, and the legal sections are embedded in a larger story of relationship, purpose, and ethics. That is why modern Jewish translations, such as the JPS, keep "Torah" or use "teaching" or "instruction."

answer:
The Hebrew morning prayer is called *Shacharit* (שחרית). It is the first of the three daily prayer services. People often mean one of two things by the question: the name and structure of the service, or the English of its opening words. I cover both below.

## Key Takeaways
- *Shacharit* means "morning prayer" and is recited every day.
- The Talmud gives two views of its origin: Abraham instituted it, or it parallels the morning Temple offering.
- It begins with *Modeh Ani*, a short thanksgiving said on waking.
- Its core is the *Shema* and its blessings, followed by the *Amidah* (standing prayer).
- Wording varies by nusach (Ashkenaz, Sefard, Edot HaMizrach, Chabad), so check your own siddur.

## Origin
[Berakhot 26b] records a dispute about where the daily prayers come from:
- Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Chanina says the Patriarchs instituted them. The Gemara says Abraham instituted the morning prayer, based on "And Abraham rose early in the morning to the place where he had stood" ([Genesis 19:27]).
- Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi says the prayers parallel the daily Temple offerings. Shacharit corresponds to the morning *tamid* offering.

## Outline of Shacharit
This is the general order. The details differ by nusach.
1. **Modeh Ani and morning blessings.** These are thanks for waking up, for health, and for the Torah.
2. **Pesukei D'Zimra** (Verses of Praise). These are psalms, including Psalm 145 (*Ashrei*) and Psalms 146–150.
3. **Shema and its blessings.** The *Shema* is "Hear, O Israel, the Lord is our God, the Lord is one" ([Deuteronomy 6:4]).
4. **Amidah.** This is the silent standing prayer, which has 19 blessings on weekdays.
5. **Concluding sections.** These include Tachanun, Torah reading on certain days, *Aleinu*, and the Kaddish prayers.

## A sample: *Modeh Ani*
